question_text: A researcher found that movements of the intestinal muscles start at one particular point spontaneously, and then it spreads to other sites. This start point of spontaneous movement is known as pacemaker. Pacemaker of the GIT is located in:
explanation:
The pacemaker cells, also known as interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs), are located in the myenteric plexus of the GI tract. The ICCs generate slow waves, which are electrical impulses that cause the smooth muscles of the GI tract to contract. The pacemaker cells are located in the fundus of the stomach, and they send slow waves to the rest of the GI tract. The slow waves travel down the GI tract, causing the muscles to contract in a coordinated manner. This coordinated contraction of the muscles is what propels food through the GI tract.

Option A is incorrect because the cardiac end of the stomach is not located in the myenteric plexus. The cardiac end of the stomach is the part of the stomach that connects to the esophagus, and it is not involved in generating slow waves.

Option B is incorrect because the pyloric end of the stomach is not located in the myenteric plexus. The pyloric end of the stomach is the part of the stomach that connects to the small intestine, and it is not involved in generating slow waves.

Option C is incorrect because the central control of CBD origin is not located in the myenteric plexus. The central control of CBD origin is a part of the brain that controls the autonomic nervous system, but it is not involved in generating slow waves.

Reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition, Page Number 787-788.

question_text: A 5-month-old infant presented to the OPD with seizures, hypotonia and hyporeflexia, and neurodevelopmental delay. This syndrome is a rare inherited disorder characterized by absent peroxisomal enzymes in all tissues leading to accumulation of C26 - C38 poly ionic acids in the brain tissue

question_text: All are features of a normal venous doppler except?
explanation:
The correct answer is: A) Triphasic patter

A normal venous Doppler typically does not exhibit a triphasic pattern. Triphasic flow patterns are commonly seen in arterial Doppler studies, not in venous Doppler studies. Venous Doppler studies typically demonstrate a continuous, unidirectional flow with variations in response to maneuvers like Valsalva and distal compression.

Indications for arterial Doppler studies presented as concise bullet points:

  • Peripheral arterial disease (PAD)
  • Evaluation of arterial stenosis or occlusion
  • Assessment of arterial aneurysms
  • Preoperative assessment before vascular surgeries
  • Evaluation of trauma-related arterial injuries
  • Monitoring vascular procedures such as angioplasty
  • Assessment of arterial bypass grafts

Here are the indications for venous Doppler studies presented as concise bullet points:

  • Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) assessment
  • Evaluation of chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)
  • Assessment of venous reflux and varicose veins
  • Screening for venous thromboembolism (VTE)
  • Monitoring of venous disorders during pregnancy
  • Assessment of vascular access for dialysis or catheter placement
  • Evaluation of post-thrombotic syndrome
  • Assessment of venous tumors or masses

Subdural Hematoma (SDH):

  • Appearance on Imaging: On imaging studies (such as CT scans), SDH appears as a crescent-shaped collection of blood that follows the contours of the brain.
  • Location: SDH occurs between the dura mater (the outermost layer of the meninges) and the arachnoid mater (the middle layer).
  • Cause: It is often caused by the tearing of bridging veins that connect the surface of the brain to the dura mater. Trauma, such as a blow to the head, is a common cause.
  • Onset: SDH can have a slower onset, and symptoms may not manifest immediately after the injury.
  • Symptoms: Symptoms may include headaches, confusion, drowsiness, and neurological deficits. Severe cases can lead to coma and death if not treated promptly.

Epidural Hematoma (EDH):

  • Appearance on Imaging: On imaging studies, EDH appears as a lens-shaped or biconvex collection of blood that does not follow the contours of the brain.
  • Location: EDH occurs between the inner surface of the skull and the dura mater.
  • Cause: It is often caused by arterial bleeding, typically from a torn middle meningeal artery, which is more frequently associated with a skull fracture.
  • Onset: EDH can have a more rapid onset compared to SDH, and symptoms may develop quickly after the injury.
  • Symptoms: Symptoms may include a lucid interval (a period of consciousness followed by deterioration), headache, vomiting, and neurological deficits. Severe cases can lead to coma and death if not treated promptly.

question_text: A patient presented with a history of unilateral weakness and difficulty in speech. He was advised to undergo a CT scan of the head which is shown below. What is shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a hyperdense appearance of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) on a non-contrast CT scan, indicating acute thrombotic occlusion of the vessel. This "dense MCA sign" is one of the earliest radiologic indicators of acute ischemic stroke.

1. Dense Artery Sign: Visible on CT as early as the onset of the stroke, indicating fresh thrombus in the vessel.

  • Proximal MCA or Terminal ICA: Associated with larger infarcts and poorer outcomes.
  • MCA Branch (Sylvian Fissure Dot Sign) (Option C): If limited to a branch, the prognosis may be better.

2. Basilar Artery: Can also show density changes in cases of posterior circulation infarcts, particularly with "top of basilar" syndrome.

3. Early Parenchymal Changes: Include reduced grey matter density and brain swelling, which may be seen as effacement of sulci referred to as insular ribbon sign (loss of gray white matter differentiation along the insular cortex). (Option A)

These findings are crucial for early diagnosis and management of stroke patients.

question_text: Identify the structure marked in the image
explanation:
Image description:

T1wI mid-Sagittal image of brain. With cerebellum marked with red arrow.

Midline sagittal image of brain showing embryonal divisions.

Mid-sagittal MR section shows the entire length of the corpus callosum bordered above by the pericallosal sulcus. Cingulate gyrus and sulcus lie above it. The brainstem divisions, cerebellar vermis and the sellar/suprasellar anatomy are exquisitely shown on this section. The vein of Galen and straight sinus are seen behind the splenium leading to the torcula. A large rounded mass of gray matter within the 3rd ventricle represents interthalamic adhesion. The fornix is seen beneath the corpus callosum. The 3rd and 4th ventricles with the interconnecting aqueduct are well shown in this section. The tectal plate lies posterior to the aqueduct. The suprasellar cistern interpeduncular fossa, quadrigeminal plate cistern and cisterna magna are important cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces identified in this section.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

  • Choice A: Cerebrum
    • The cerebrum comprises the largest part of the brain, including the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes.
    • It is located above the cerebellum and is responsible for higher cognitive functions such as thinking, memory, and voluntary movements.
    • The marked structure does not correspond to the cerebrum.
  • Choice C: Brainstem
    • The brainstem consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla and connects the cerebrum and spinal cord.
    • It is anterior to the cerebellum in a midsagittal section.
    • The marked structure is not the brainstem.
  • Choice D: Corpus Callosum
    • The corpus callosum is the largest white matter tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
    • It is located superior to the cerebellum and brainstem, forming a C-shaped structure in the mid-sagittal view.
    • The marked structure does not correspond to the corpus callosum.

Key takeaway:

This is the must know section of the radiological anatomy of brain.

question_text: A 60 yr old patient came with inability to bear weight following a trivial trauma and the following finding on the PBH and thigh x rays. She has a history of weight loss. Whatis the most likely diagnosis?

Image Description:

Explanation:-

Skeletal metastases are defined as tumors involving bone, which originate from another distal site.

Metastases are the most common malignant tumors of the skeletal system. Approximately 70% of all malignant tumors are metastatic in origin, with only 30% being primary in nature.

The most common primary sites are in the breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid, and bowel. With the exception of tumors of the central nervous system and basal cell carcinoma of the skin, almost every malignant tumor can metastasize to bone.

Bone involvement in metastases occurs by means of three main mechanisms:

(1) direct extension,

(2) retrograde venous flow

(3) seeding with tumor emboli via the blood circulation which is the most common route of spread.

Age

Most patients are older than 40 years. In children <5 years, skeletal metastases usually occur from neuroblastoma. Metastases between the age group of 10 and 25 years commonly occur from Ewing sarcoma and osteosarcoma, and between 20 and 35 years, they occur from Hodgkin lymphoma.

Sex

In females, the carcinoma of the breast is responsible for majority of all bone metastases followed by the carcinomas of thyroid, kidney, and uterus. In males, carcinoma prostate is the most common primary focus, followed by the carcinoma of the lung.

Site

They are most often found in the axial skeleton and other sites of residual red marrow. Thus, the common sites for metastases are vertebrae, pelvis, proximal femora and humeri, skull, sternum, and ribs. Metastases to bones of hand and feet are rare and almost 50% of these are due to the carcinoma of the lung.

Clinical Picture

The lesions may be entirely asymptomatic or present with vague bone pains. Occasionally, a pathological fracture through the metastatic lesion may bring it to notice. Weight loss, cachexia, anemia, and even fever may be seen in the later stages.

Imaging Features

Plain Radiographs

Bone metastases may be lytic, sclerotic, or mixed lytic and sclerotic. As a metastatic lesion grows in the medullary cavity, the surrounding bone is remodeled by means of either osteoclastic or osteoblastic processes.

The majority (75%) of metastases is osteolytic. Some metastases (15%) are predominantly osteoblastic, e.g., from prostate, stomach, and carcinoid. Mixed osteolytic and osteosclerotic metastasis (10%) occur from carcinoma of the breast and occasionally, lung.

In females, the carcinoma of the breast is responsible for majority of all bone metastases followed by the carcinomas of thyroid, kidney, and uterus. In males, carcinoma prostate is the most common primary focus, followed by the carcinoma of the lung.

Incorrect choices explanation :

Choice A:- Eosinophilic granuloma :- Well defined lytic lesion with beveled age, usually seen in the child age group, can involve axial flat bones as well as long bones.

Choice B :- Osteoarticular tuberculosis can occur in the spine, hip, knee, foot, elbow, wrist, hand, shoulder and as diaphyseal foci. It has not been reported to affect the mandible or the temporomandibular joint. The major method of spread is hematogenous. The most common method of spread to the vertebral body is through the Batson's venous plexus.

Choice C :- Brown tumors are usually multiple in number, associated with other features of hyperparathyroidism like bone resorption (sub-periosteal , intracortical,etc.)

Key takeaway:-

  • Metastases are the most common malignant tumors of the skeletal system. Approximately 70% of all malignant tumors are metastatic in origin, with only 30% being primary in nature.
  • The majority (75%) of metastases is osteolytic. Some metastases (15%) are predominantly osteoblastic, e.g., from prostate, stomach, and carcinoid. Mixed osteolytic and osteosclerotic metastasis (10%) occur from carcinoma of the breast and occasionally, lung.
  • In females, the carcinoma of the breast is responsible for majority of all bone metastases followed by the carcinomas of thyroid, kidney, and uterus.
  • In males, carcinoma prostate is the most common primary focus, followed by the carcinoma of the lung.

Lacunar infarcts (LACI) are small (<15 mm) infarcts in the distal distribution of deep penetrating vessels (lenticulostriate, thalamo-perforating, and pontine perforating arteries, recurrent artery of Heubner). They result from occlusion of one of the small penetrating end arteries at the base of the brain and have traditionally been thought to occur due to fibrinoid degeneration.

Most lacunar infarcts are clinically silent, but repeated episodes are associated with vascular dementia. Symptomatic patients may present with lacunar stroke syndrome, one of five distinct syndromes.

CT Findings:

In the acute setting, lacunar infarcts appear as ill-defined hypodensities.

Chronic lesions appear as hypodense foci, similar density to CSF.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Normal: hypodensity in left thalamic region is not a normal finding.

Choice C: Basal ganglia bleed: Bleed on NCCT appears as a hyperdense area, with decreasing hyper-density according to the age of hemorrhage.

Choice D: intraventricular hemorrhage: Shows hyperdense area in dependent portion of the ventricles.

Key takeaway:

  • Lacunar infarcts (LACI) are small (<15 mm) infarcts in the distal distribution of deep penetrating vessels.
  • CT Findings:
    In the acute setting, lacunar infarcts appear as ill-defined hypodensities.
    Chronic lesions appear as hypodense foci, similar density to CSF.

question_text: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the OPD with a parietal swelling that has been present since birth. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray image shows a localized, well-defined swelling over the parietal region not crossing suture lines. Cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal hemorrhage confined by suture lines, presenting as a firm, well-circumscribed swelling over the parietal bone.

  • Cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal collection of blood that occurs due to rupture of blood vessels between the skull and periosteum.
  • It typically presents within the first few hours of life, grows over 12-24 hours, and is limited by suture lines, as the periosteum is tightly adherent at these borders.
  • The swelling is firm, well-circumscribed, and located most commonly over the parietal bones.
  • It may take weeks to resolve, and in some cases, may lead to hyperbilirubinemia or be associated with linear skull fractures.

Explanation of other options:

Subgaleal hematoma (Option A): A more diffuse hemorrhage in the subaponeurotic space that crosses suture lines and is often associated with significant blood loss and hemodynamic instability.

Encephalocele (Option D): A neural tube defect presenting as a sac-like protrusion of brain tissue through a skull defect, typically requiring neurosurgical intervention.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option C): Bleeding into the subarachnoid space; CT reveals diffuse blood in the sulci, cisterns, or ventricles, classically presenting with sudden "worst headache of life."

explanation:
Explanation:

Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS), also known as encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, is a neurocutaneous disorder characterized by facial port-wine nevus and pial angiomas. It is primarily associated with the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve and shows characteristic serpiginous gyriform calcification.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Facial Nevus: Congenital port-wine stain, often present at birth.
  • Neurological Symptoms: Seizures, developmental delays, and possible hemiparesis, particularly related to cortical involvement.

Radiological Findings:

Plain Radiography:

  • Gyriform Calcification: Typically becomes evident between ages 2-7.

CT Imaging:

  • Subcortical Calcifications: Early identification of calcifications compared to plain films.
  • Tram-Track Sign: Represents cortical and subcortical calcifications.
  • Volume Loss: Associated parenchymal volume loss may be visible.
  • Enlargement: Calvarial and regional sinus enlargement may occur.
  • Choroid Plexus: Ipsilateral enlargement may be noted.
  • Dyke-Davidoff-Masson Appearance: In severe cases, this appearance indicates hemispheric atrophy.
  • Orbital Choroidal Hemangiomas: May be present.
  • Cavernous Sinus: Asymmetric enlargement may be evident.

MRI Findings:

  • T1-weighted Images:
    • Generally normal signal in the affected region, with volume loss evident at older ages.
    • Gadolinium Enhancement: Prominent leptomeningeal enhancement due to venous congestion and ischemia.
  • T2-weighted Images:
    • Low signal in white matter subjacent to the angioma, possibly indicating accelerated myelination in neonates.
    • Later calcification may be present.
    • Abnormal Venous Drainage: Flow voids may be seen.
  • Advanced Techniques:
    • Gradient Echo (GE)/Susceptibility Weighted Imaging (SWI): Sensitive to calcifications, showing regions of signal dropout.
    • MR Spectroscopy: Typically shows decreased N-acetyl aspartate (NAA), indicating neuronal loss.

Calcification of the thalami (Option A): Seen in conditions like TORCH infections (especially CMV or toxoplasmosis), not in Sturge-Weber syndrome.

Dentate calcification (Option B): Involves the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum, classically seen in Fahr’s disease or chronic anticonvulsant therapy, not in this condition.

Intraventricular hemorrhage (Option D): Usually occurs in premature infants due to germinal matrix bleed, unrelated to the cortical vascular malformation seen in Sturge-Weber syndrome.

question_text: A 3-year-old patient presented with recurrent urinary tract infections. On eliciting history, there was some difficulty while passing urine. He was advised to undergo a MCU examination. It is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The MCU (Micturating Cystourethrogram) image shows retrograde opacification of the ureter and pelvicalyceal system during bladder filling and voiding phase, indicating reflux of contrast from bladder into the ureters and kidneys. → These findings are classic for Vesicoureteric Reflux (VUR).

Vesico-ureteric reflux (VUR) is the abnormal flow of urine from the bladder back into the upper urinary tract (ureters and kidneys). It is most commonly seen in young children and is associated with an increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and pyelonephritis.

Diagnostic Procedures

  1. Voiding Cystourethrogram (VCUG):
    • The primary diagnostic method for evaluating VUR. This fluoroscopic procedure involves filling the bladder with contrast and taking images while the child voids, allowing assessment of reflux.
  2. Other Diagnostic Methods:
    • Nuclear Medicine Studies:
      • MAG3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine): Useful as a screening tool, especially in older patients, to evaluate renal function and detect reflux.
    • Ultrasound:
      • Can assess for hydronephrosis and other anatomical abnormalities but is less sensitive for detecting reflux compared to VCUG.
    • MR Voiding Cystography:
      • An emerging non-invasive technique that uses MRI to visualize the bladder and assess for reflux.
  • PUJ obstruction will have ballooning of only pelvis and normal ureters.
  • Horseshoe kidney shows hand holding sign on IVP
  • duplex pelvicalyceal system, two renal pelvis and ureters are noted.

Explanation of Other options:

PUJO (Pelvi-ureteric Junction Obstruction) (Option A): On MCU, the ureter is not opacified because reflux doesn't occur. Diagnosis is typically made on IVP or renal scan, showing pelvicalyceal dilatation with abrupt narrowing at PUJ, not seen here.

Horseshoe kidneys (Option C): A fusion anomaly seen on ultrasound or IVP, where lower poles of both kidneys are joined across midline. MCU does not demonstrate the isthmus or the characteristic renal malrotation.

Duplex pelvicalyceal system (Option D): Shows two ureters draining a single kidney, sometimes with ureterocele or differential reflux. Here, only single ureters are seen with reflux of contrast, ruling out duplication.

question_text: Dawson Fingers are feature of
explanation:
Periventricular white matter hyperintensities perpendicular to ventricles are called Dawsons fingers seen in Multiple Sclerosis

The McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis (MS) are used to diagnose MS and provide guidelines for clinicians. They incorporate clinical, imaging, and laboratory findings to determine the likelihood of MS. The criteria were updated in 2017 to include the following:

  1. Dissemination in space (DIS): Evidence of lesions in different areas of the central nervous system (CNS), including the brain, optic nerves, and spinal cord.
  2. Dissemination in time (DIT): Evidence of new lesions appearing over time on follow-up MRI scans, or a simultaneous presence of gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions at any time.
  3. Clinical presentation: Symptoms suggestive of MS, such as optic neuritis, myelitis, or brainstem and cerebellar syndromes.
  4. Supporting laboratory findings: Oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid, which indicate an immune response within the CNS.
  5. Additional MRI criteria: The presence of specific lesions (such as juxtacortical, periventricular, or infratentorial lesions) on MRI scans.

The McDonald criteria allow for a more timely and accurate diagnosis of MS, enabling earlier initiation of treatment and better management of the disease.

question_text: Which of the following is seen in pelvic inflammatory disease in fallopian tubes?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) refers to a spectrum of infections and inflammatory conditions affecting the upper female genital tract, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries.

Etiology

PID is often caused by sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as:

  • Chlamydia trachomatis
  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Other non-STI pathogens can also contribute to PID, particularly after surgical procedures or childbirth.

Clinical Presentation

Symptoms of PID can vary widely and may include:

  • Lower abdominal pain
  • Abnormal vaginal discharge
  • Fever
  • Pain during intercourse
  • Irregular menstrual bleeding

Key Ultrasound Findings

  1. Distinction from Fluid-Filled Bowel LoopsbyLack of Peristalsis,a dilated fallopian tube will not exhibit peristalsis.
  2. Low-Level Internal Echoesmay indicate the presence of pus (pyosalpinx).
  3. HydrosalpinxshowsAnechoic Fluid
  4. Tubal Wall Thickness:A wall thickness of ≥5 mm suggests acute disease.

Tubal Wall Structures

  • Cogwheel Sign:
    • An anechoic "cogwheel-shaped" appearance in cross-section, indicative of thickened walls, primarily seen in acute disease.
  • Beads on a String Sign:
  • Hyperechoic mural nodules (2-3 mm) on cross-section of a distended tube, seen in chronic disease due to degenerated endosalpingeal folds.
  • Incomplete Septa:
  • Hyperechoic septa protruding from one wall but not reaching the opposite wall; observed in both acute and chronic disease but not discriminatory.

Waist Sign (Patel et al. Findings)

  • Tubular Fluid-Filled Mass:
  • Characterized by diametrically opposed indentations in the wall, referred to as the "waist sign." This sign has the highest likelihood ratio for distinguishing hydrosalpinx from other adnexal masses.

question_text:
A 40-year-old comes to the physician with a 2-month history of exertional dyspnea and progressive lower extremity swelling. He also reports abdominal distension and decreased appetite. The patient has gained 4.5 kg over the last 2 months. Past medical history is significant for hypertension and recurrent lung infections requiring prolonged antibiotic therapy. He has no history of coronary artery disease. The patient smokes a pack of cigarettes daily for the past 15 years. He undergoes noninvasive cardiac testing followed by cardiac catheterization. A jugular venous pressure tracing is shown on the slide below.

The waveform indicated by the arrow most likely corresponds to which of the following?
option_d: Tricuspid valve bulging into the right atrium
explanation:
A normal jugular venous pulse wave tracing has 3 positive waves (a, c, and v) and 2 negative waves (x and y descent). The a wave (indicated by the arrow on the diagram above) is generated by atrial contraction, the c wave is caused by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium in early systole, and the v wave reflects the passive increase in pressure and volume of the right atrium as it fills in late systole and early diastole. The troughs of the jugular venous pulse are known as the x-descent and the y-descent. The x-descent is primarily caused by relaxation of the right atrium. The y-descent represents the abrupt decrease in right atrial pressure during early diastole after the tricuspid valve opens and the right ventricle begins to passively fill.

Option A: Atrial contraction generates a wave of JVP.

Option B: Carotid pulse upstroke has some minor contribution in c wave, but major factor is bulging of the tricuspid valve in the right atrium.

Option C: The x-descent is primarily caused by relaxation of the right atrium.

Reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition, Page Number-119.

question_text: A 34-year-old patient presented to the surgeon with complaints of tiredness, shortness of breath, frequent infections & bleeding. On examination, he was having splenomegaly and painless lumps in arms & neck areas. Pathological findings are depicted in the figure below, and are suggestive of hairy cell leukemia. Which among the following is the drug of choice for treatment of hairy cell leukemia?
explanation:
Cladribine is an ADA-resistant purine analogue that has potent and curative activity in hairy cell leukemia, CLL, and low-grade lymphomas. Cladribine is resistant to degradation by adenosine deaminase, hence, it is the drug of choice for the treatment of hairy cell leukemia.

Cladribine is administered daily for 7 days by continuous intravenous infusion. It is the drug of choice in hairy cell leukemia. Eighty percent of the patients achieve complete response after a single course of therapy. The drug is also active in CLL, low-grade lymphomas, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, CTCLs including mycosis fungoides and the Sezary syndrome; and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.

Adverse Effects-

The major dose-limiting toxicity of cladribine is myelosuppression. Cumulative thrombocytopenia may occur with repeated courses. Opportunistic infections are common and correlate with decreased CD4+ cell counts. Other toxic effects include nausea, infections, high fever, headache, fatigue, skin rashes, and tumor lysis syndrome.

Reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th Edition, Page Number-1185.

question_text: Signet Ring Appearance on HRCT suggests?
explanation:
Signet Ring Appearance and TramTrack Appearance

On Hrct is suggestive Of Bronchiectasis

High-resolution CT (HRCT) is sensitive for detecting bronchiectasis. Signs of bronchiectasis on HRCT include:

  1. Dilated and Irregular Bronchi:
    • Enlarged and distorted airways, often seen as dilated bronchi with thickened walls.
  2. Tram-Tracking Sign:
    • Parallel linear opacities along the dilated bronchi, resembling tram tracks.
  3. Cylinder and Signet Ring Signs:
    • Cross-sectional images may show cylindrical or tubular bronchi (cylinder sign) and dilated bronchi with surrounding collapsed lung (signet ring sign).
  4. Tree-in-Bud Pattern:
    • Small branching opacities representing impacted mucus-filled bronchioles.
  5. Atelectasis or Consolidation:
    • Due to bronchial obstruction, leading to distal lung collapse or consolidation.
  6. Mucous Plugging:
    • Accumulation of mucus in dilated bronchi, contributing to airway obstruction.
  7. Bronchial Wall Thickening:
    • Thickened bronchial walls, often seen in chronic bronchiectasis.
  8. Varicose Bronchiectasis:
    • Irregular, beaded appearance of bronchi, resembling varicose veins.
  9. Ground-Glass Opacities:
    • May be present due to inflammation or infection associated with bronchiectasis.

Recognition of these features helps in diagnosing bronchiectasis on HRCT, allowing for appropriate management and treatment planning.

Causes of bronchiectasis:

  1. Infections:
    • Recurrent respiratory infections (bacterial, fungal, viral).
  2. Immunodeficiency Disorders:
    • Primary immunodeficiencies (e.g., common variable immunodeficiency).
    • Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
  3. Cystic Fibrosis:
    • Genetic disorder affecting CFTR gene, leading to impaired mucus clearance.
  4. Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA):
    • Fungal infection triggering hypersensitivity reactions (common in asthmatics).
  5. Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency:
    • Genetic deficiency predisposing to lung tissue damage.
  6. Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD):
    • Genetic disorder affecting cilia function, impairing mucociliary clearance.
  7. Connective Tissue Disorders:
    • Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus.
  8. Foreign Body Aspiration:
    • Inhalation of foreign objects causing chronic inflammation.
  9. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD):
    • Repeated microaspiration of gastric contents due to GERD.
  10. Tuberculosis:
    • Previous or active tuberculosis infection causing bronchial damage.
  11. Autoimmune Diseases:
    • Wegener's granulomatosis, rheumatoid arthritis affecting the respiratory system.
  12. Airway Obstruction:
    • Tumors, bronchial strictures, inhaled objects causing persistent obstruction.

question_text: Most common CP Angle tumor is?
explanation:
• CP angle tumors
  • acoustic schwannoma: most common
  • meningioma: second most common
  • trigeminal schwannoma
  • facial nerve schwannoma
  • ependymoma
  • metastasis, e.g. breast, lung, malignant melanoma

The differential diagnosis for a mass in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) on radiological imaging includes various benign and malignant entities. Some common differentials include:

  1. Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma): This is the most common CPA tumor. It arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve and typically presents with gradual hearing loss and tinnitus.
  2. Meningioma: A slow-growing tumor arising from the meninges, which can occur at the CPA and compress adjacent structures.
  3. Epidermoid Cyst: A benign tumor arising from ectodermal remnants, which can appear similar to CSF on imaging.
  4. Arachnoid Cyst: A benign cyst arising from the arachnoid membrane, often asymptomatic but can cause symptoms if large enough to compress adjacent structures.
  5. Metastasis: Tumors from distant sites can metastasize to the CPA, although this is less common than primary CPA tumors.
  6. Cholesteatoma: An abnormal collection of skin cells in the middle ear, which can erode into the CPA and cause symptoms.
  7. Facial Nerve Schwannoma: A rare tumor arising from the Schwann cells of the facial nerve, which can present with facial weakness.
  8. Paraganglioma (Glomus Jugulare Tumor): A rare, highly vascular tumor arising from paraganglionic tissue in the jugular foramen, which can extend into the CPA.

Differentiation among these entities often requires advanced imaging techniques such as MRI with contrast and clinical correlation. Biopsy or surgical resection may be necessary for definitive diagnosis in some cases.

question_text: Drop Metastasis due to CSF spread is seen with all except?
explanation:
Drop metastasis refers to the spread of tumor cells through the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leading to seeding of the leptomeninges along the spinal cord or brain surface. This phenomenon is seen in certain types of brain tumors, particularly those originating in or near the ventricles or meninges.

  • Medulloblastoma (A), Pineal germinoma (B), and Ependymoblastoma (C) are all types of brain tumors that can spread through the CSF and cause drop metastasis.
  • Oligodendroglioma (D), however, typically does not exhibit this pattern of spread. Oligodendrogliomas are more likely to spread locally within the brain rather than through the CSF.

question_text: Intradermal injection of histamine and bradykinin to a mouse evoked dose dependent hyperalgesia. Which of the following prostaglandins is responsible for such a response?
explanation:
Option B - PGE2 is hyperalgesic, making the skin hypersensitive to painful stimuli such as intradermal injection of suboptimal concentrations of histamine and bradykinin. It is involved in cytokine-induced fever during infections.

Option A - PGD2 is the major prostaglandin made by mast cells; along with PGE2 (which is more widely distributed), it causes vasodilation and increases the permeability of postcapillary venules, thus potentiating edema formation. PGD2 also is a chemoattractant for neutrophils.

Option C - Prostacyclin is a vasodilator and a potent inhibitor of platelet aggregation, and also markedly potentiates the permeability-increasing and chemotactic effects of other mediators. A thromboxane-prostacyclin imbalance has been implicated as an early event in thrombus formation in coronary and cerebral blood vessels.

Option D - TxA2, a potent platelet-aggregating agent and vasoconstrictor, is itself unstable and rapidly converted to its inactive form. Vascular endothelium lacks thromboxane synthase but contains prostacyclin synthase, which is responsible for the formation of prostacyclin (PGI2) and its stable end product PGF1a.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page Number-87.

question_text: In a research aimed at studying the role of IFN-γ, it is concluded that IFN-γ activates macrophages, which have an important role in forming immune granulomas. Which of the following CD4 T cells secrete this cytokine IFN-γ
explanation:
Option B - Th1 cells produce the cytokine IFN-γ, which activates macrophages by the classical pathway. Immune granulomas are caused by a variety of agents that are capable of inducing a persistent T cell-mediated immune response. This type of immune response usually produces granulomas when the inciting agent is difficult to eradicate, such as a persistent microbe. In such responses, activated Th1 cells produce cytokines such as IFN-γ, which activates macrophages. In some parasitic infections, such as schistosomiasis, the granulomas are associated with strong Th2 responses and eosinophils.

Option A - Th17 cells secrete IL-17 and other cytokines, which induce the secretion of chemokines responsible for recruiting neutrophils (and monocytes) into the reaction.

Option C - Th2 cells secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, which recruit and activate eosinophils and are responsible for the alternative pathway of macrophage activation.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page Number 99-100.

question_text: A 10-month-old girl had recurrent infections affecting various systems. All immunoglobulins were found to be reduced. Which of the following is not a characteristic seen in classic agammaglobulinemia?
option_a: Serum levels of all classes of immunoglobulins are decreased.
option_b: Absent plasma cells throughout the body.
option_c: Germinal centers of lymph nodes, peyer's patches and tonsils are underdeveloped.
explanation:
The classic form of this disease has the following characteristics:

  • B cells are absent or markedly decreased in the circulation, and serum levels of all classes of immunoglobulins are depressed. Pre B cells, which express the B-lineage marker CD19 but not membrane Ig, are found in normal numbers in the bone marrow.
  • Germinal centers of lymph nodes, peyer's patches, the appendix, and tonsils are underdeveloped.
  • Plasma cells are absent throughout the body.
  • T cell mediated reactions are normal.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page Number-244.

question_text: A patient presented with gradual onset of deafness. On further investigation it was found to be of sensorineural type and was advised to undergo an MRI examination. The following image was obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows bilateral vestibular (acoustic) schwannomas appearing as enhancing masses in the cerebellopontine angles on MRI. This finding is pathognomonic of NF2. These tumors arise from the Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) and cause bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is caused by mutations in the NF2 gene located on chromosome 22, which encodes the protein merlin. It is a rare autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder characterized by the development of multiple central nervous system (CNS) tumors.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Typical Age of Onset: Usually presents in young adults, typically between ages 18-24.
  • Common Tumors:
    • Vestibular Schwannomas (Acoustic Neuromas): Often bilateral and can lead to hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance issues.
    • Meningiomas: Can be located intracranially or in the spinal canal.
    • Ependymomas: Frequently found in the spinal cord.

Symptoms:

  • Hearing loss, balance difficulties, headaches, and neurological deficits, depending on the location and size of tumors.

Imaging Modality: MRI is the preferred method for evaluating CNS tumors associated with NF2 due to its superior soft tissue contrast.

NF1 (Option A): NF1 is characterized by optic gliomas, café-au-lait spots, and neurofibromas, not by bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

VHL (Option C): Von Hippel Lindau disease is an Autosomal Dominant disorder with deletion of VHL gene on chromosome 3p. It characterized by Hemangioblastoma, Capillary hemangiomas, Renal cell carcinomas and Pheochromocytomas.

TS (Option D): Tuberous sclerosis is an Autosomal Dominant disorder with TSC1 gene(hamartin) mutation on chromosome 9 and TSC2 (tuberin) mutation on chromosome 16.

question_text: A 7-year-old boy presents with a history of repeated urinary tract infections, a weak urinary stream, and failure to thrive. On examination, his abdomen appears distended, and a palpable bladder is noted. The micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) is shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The child's presentation with recurrent UTIs, poor stream, distended abdomen, palpable bladder, and poor growth is characteristic of posterior urethral valves (PUV), a congenital condition causing urinary tract obstruction in male children.

MCU (Micturating Cystourethrogram) findings in PUV:

  • Dilated posterior urethra
  • Thickened bladder wall
  • Possible vesicoureteral reflux

Ultrasound features:

  • Classic keyhole sign, due to dilation of the posterior urethra and a distended bladder

Management:

  • Cystoscopic valve ablation is the initial and definitive treatment. It involves endoscopic removal of the obstructive posterior urethral valves, thus relieving the obstruction and preventing progressive renal damage.

Explanation for other options:

Urethral reconstruction (Option B): Reserved for cases where obstruction persists or in severe damage post-ablation; not first-line.

Intermittent catheterisation (Option C): May offer short-term relief, but doesn't resolve the anatomical obstruction.

Bladder augmentation surgery (Option D): Used in conditions like neurogenic bladder with small capacity, not in primary obstructive disorders like PUV.

Reference:

  1. Posterior urethral valves
  2. Keyhole sign (posterior urethral valves)

question_text: A case of allergic rhinitis, NCCT image of paranasal air sinuses shows an appearance known as?
explanation:
Image description:

Coronal CT image of PNS shows soft tissue density area within the left nasal cavity with central hyperdensity within, k/a Double density sign. Classical for Allergic fungal rhino-sinusitis.

Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis

It occurs as an allergic response to fungal elements in atopic patients. On CT, diffuse mucosal thickening involving multiple sinuses is present. Within the sinus there may be central hyperdense content and peripheral hypodensity.

Bony destruction is usually not seen. Calcification is also a common finding in fungal infections especially with aspergillosis. Central or fine punctate pattern of calcification is characteristic of fungal infection. Many patients may have polyps.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Honeycombing: Honeycombing represents the destruction of lung parenchyma with loss of architecture and well-defined adjacent cystic structures, typically clustered in the subpleural region. The traditional definition requires several layers of cysts, but in current practice, this threshold has been reduced to a single layer of cysts, provided other signs of fibrosis are present. The diameter and wall thickness of the cysts are variable but their presence is inevitably accompanied by the complete effacement of normal lung architecture and usually occurs with other signs of pulmonary fibrosis, including traction bronchiolectasis.

Choice C: Onion peel appearance: it is a type of aggressive periosteal reaction seen in malignant bone tumors i.e. Ewings sarcoma.

Choice D: Ground glass opacity. Ground-glass refers to an area of increased attenuation that does not completely obscure the underlying bronchial and vascular structures. Although historically first described on radiographs specifics of this term have been defined for CT and it should only be applied in the context of CT. The finding is nonspecific, as ground-glass can be caused by any abnormal process below the resolution of the CT scanner that does not completely displace alveolar air, for example, partial filling of alveoli by fluid or cellular material, an increase in capillary blood volume, histologic fibrosis, a lepidic pattern of adenocarcinoma, or a combination of the above.

Key takeaway:

Double density sign in PNS CT: Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis

question_text: Incorrect statement regarding the condition given in the image is?
option_b: Tumour arises from epiphyseal to metaphyseal region
option_c: Chemotherapy is the treatment of choice
explanation:
Image description:

Radiograph of the knee shows an eccentric expansile subarticular lytic lesion in distal end of femur without sclerotic margin.

Giant cell tumor constitutes about 5% of all bone tumors and slightly less than 20% of all benign tumors. The tumor originates from undifferentiated cells of the supporting tissues of bone marrow. As opposed to other benign tumors, GCT has a female predilection and mostly occurs after the closure of epiphysis, with a peak in the third decade.

Giant cell tumors arise eccentrically in the metaphysis with tendency to approach the adjacent subarticular cortex as they enlarge. About 40-50% of lesions occur around the knee.

Involvement of distal radius is seen in 10-12% which otherwise is an uncommon site for bone tumors.

Other sites are sacrum, short tubular bones, and vertebral bodies. Classical radiographic picture is that of a well-defined eccentric lytic lesion which expands the bone and is usually not surrounded by a sclerotic rim. Cortical penetration with or without an associated soft tissue mass is seen in 33-50% of cases.

Treatment is usually done by the curettage and bone cementing. Chemotherapy is usually not indicated as it is a benign tumor.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

  • Choice A: Sharp distinct border (Correct Statement)
    • GCT typically presents as an eccentric, well-defined, lytic lesion.
    • It often lacks a sclerotic rim, giving it a sharp, distinct border.
  • Choice B: Tumor arises from epiphyseal to metaphyseal region (Correct Statement)
    • GCT arises in the metaphysis and extends into the epiphysis after the growth plate has closed.
    • This is a characteristic feature of the tumor.
  • Choice D: Eccentric location (Correct Statement)
    • GCT arises eccentrically in the metaphysis, meaning it does not appear in the central part of the bone.
    • It tends to grow towards the subarticular cortex.

Key takeaway:

  • GCT has a female predilection and mostly occurs after the closure of epiphysis, with a peak in the third decade.
  • Usually not surrounded by a sclerotic rim.
  • Giant cell tumors arise eccentrically in the metaphysis with tendency to approach the adjacent subarticular cortex as they enlarge.

question_text: Identify the best screening investigation for metabolic disorders.

question_text: A 5-year-old child presented with weakness and an altered gait. MRI brain was obtained as shown below. What is the diagnosis?

The MRI shows a cystic mass with an enhancing mural nodule located in the cerebellum, characteristic of pilocytic astrocytoma, a circumscribed WHO Grade I glioma.

Pilocytic astrocytoma's, also known as juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma, are circumscribed, low-grade gliomas predominantly found in children and young adults.

Epidemiology:

Most common primary brain tumor in childhood (approximately 15%) and the second most common pediatric posterior fossa tumor (about 30%), following medulloblastomas.

Clinical Features:

  • Typically present with symptoms related to increased intracranial pressure, cerebellar dysfunction, or visual disturbances, especially when located near the optic pathways.

Imaging Modality:

  • MRI is the preferred imaging technique for evaluating pilocytic astrocytoma.
    • Often contains a large cystic component with a mural nodule that enhances with contrast.
    • May show associated calcifications, but these are not always present.
    • Peritumoral edema is common and may be prominent, especially with larger tumors.

HPE:

Histopathology Appearance of pilocytic astrocytoma contains Rosenthal fibers (eosinophilic corkscrew fibers).

Hemangioblastoma (Option A): A cerebellar tumor composed of thin-walled capillaries with minimal intervening parenchyma. Also presents as cyst with mural nodule, but typically occurs in adults and is strongly associated with von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome.

Metastases (Option C): Rare in children; usually multiple and supratentorial.

Oligodendroglioma (Option D): Usually located in the frontal region; often calcified. Histologically, cells are of Fried egg appearance, and capillaries are seen in Chicken wire pattern.

question_text: A 16 year old patient presented with seizures. An MRI brain was done and revealed multiple such lesions in the brain. On MR Spectroscopy these lesions revealed elevated choline, alanine and lactate. The most likely diagnosis is?
explanation:
Cysticercosis is the commonest parasitic disease in humans caused by the worm Taenia solium. It is the most common cause of acquired epilepsy throughout the world.

There are four main stages :

  • vesicular: viable parasite with intact membrane and therefore no host
  • colloidal vesicular: parasite dies within 4-5 years 1 untreated, or earlier with treatment and the cyst fluid becomes turbid. As the membrane becomes leaky edema surrounds the cyst. This is the most symptomatic stage.
  • granular nodular: edema decreases as the cyst retract further; enhancement persists.
  • nodular calcified: end-stage quiescent calcified cyst remnant; no edema. Each stage has fairly distinctive imaging features although there is no sharp demarcation between later stages.

On imaging,

Vesicular

  • cyst with dot sign
  • CSF density/intensity
  • eccentric hyperintense scolex on Tl can sometimes be seen
  • no enhancement is typical, although very faint enhancement of the wall and enhancement of the scolex may be seen
  • no surrounding vasogenic edema

Colloidal vesicular

  • cyst fluid becomes macroscopically turbid reflected in altered imaging appearance:
    • CT: hyperattenuating to CSF
    • MRI Tl: hyperintense to CSF 2
  • surrounding edema
  • cyst and the wall become thickened and brightly enhances
  • scolex is seen early in the colloidal phase but gradually shrinks down and is harder to identify

Granular nodular

  • edema decreases
  • cyst retracts eventually becoming a small enhancing nodule
  • enhancement persists but is less marked

Nodular calcified

  • end-stage quiescent calcified nodule
  • no edema
  • no enhancement on CT
  • signal drop out on T2 and T2* sequences
  • some intrinsic high Tl signal may be present
  • long term enhancement may be evident on MRI and may predict ongoing seizures

Reference: AIIMS-MAMC-PGl's Comprehensive textbook of diagnostic radiology page 3520

question_text: A 40-year-old male is suffering from increasing difficulty in bending forward with increasing stiffness of the spine. A Ct was performed and shown below. Likely Diagnosis-
explanation:
The given xray shows bamboo spine due to osteophyte formation which is suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic, progressive inflammatory arthritis which chiefly involves the synovial joints of the spine along with the adjacent soft tissues as well as the sacroiliac joints, although peripheral, large joints such as the hips, shoulders and knee can also be involved.

Radiological features:

SI joints: The classic sacroiliitis is bilateral and symmetrical. Changes occur in both the synovial along with ligamentous (superior and posterior) parts of the sacroiliac joints.

The earliest radiographic findings occur in the subchondral cortex which appears blurred or lost.
Later, small (rat-bite) erosions appear which are worse along the iliac aspect of the joint. These cause widening of the joint space with hazy margins. This is followed by larger erosions, subjacent sclerosis and joint space narrowing as irregular new bone bridges the joint space with eventual ankylosis and resolution of the sclerosis.

The modified New York criteria is used for grading of sacroiliitis and was established in 1994.

Spine: Spinal involvement classically starts at the dorsolumbar or lumbosacral junction.
Erosions initially occur at the vertebral margins at the site of attachment of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus (Romanus lesions) with adjacent sclerosis (shiny corner sign).

Healing of these erosions or laying down of bone beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament causes "squaring" of the vertebral bodies, best appreciated on lateral radiographs of the lumbar spine.
Exuberant new bone formation may even cause anterior convexity of the vertebral body (barrel-shaped vertebrae).

Ossifications may be seen in the interspinous ligaments and facet joints causing the dagger and tram-track signs respectively.
Facet joint ankylosis is the major factor causing loss of spinal mobility.

Dagger sign

Tram Track/Trolley sign

KEY TAKEAWAY- Radiological findings in Ankylosing Spondylitis.

Calcification of anterior longitudinal ligament.

Calcification of intervertebral disc giving rise to bamboo spine//Tram track sign/Trolley sign.

Calcification of interspinous ligament- dagger sign

On MRI -lesions seen in the anterior part of intervertebral disc [Andersson lesion ].

Reference: AIIMS-MAMC-PGI'S Comprehensive textbook of diagnostic radiology page no 2830

Correct Answer: (A) Anterior Ethmoid Canal

(A) Anterior Ethmoid Canal (Correct Answer)

  • Part of the ethmoid bone forming the roof of the nasal cavity.
  • Contains multiple small foramina for the passage of olfactory nerve fibers (CN I).
  • The marked structure in the image is lateral to the cribriform plate, making this option incorrect.

question_text: Which of the following is not a criteria for PCOD?
option_b: >12 follicles in at least one ovary

explanation:
• Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), recently referred also as hyperandrogenic anovulation, is a chronic anovulation syndrome associated with androgen excess.
  • The Rotterdam criteria is used to make the diagnosis of PCOS and require any two of the following three criteria for the diagnosis, as well as the exclusion of other etiologies (e.g. congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing syndrome, and/or an androgen-secreting tumor):
  • Ovulatory dysfunction (oligo- and/or anovulation)
  • Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism
  • Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound.

A polycystic ovary on USG is defined as an ovary containing 12 or more follicles (or 25 or more follicles using new ultrasound technology) measuring 2 to 9 mm in diameter or an ovary that has a volume of greater than 10 mL on ultrasonography. A single ovary meeting either or both of these definitions is sufficient for the diagnosis of polycystic ovaries

Other morphological features have been described, but do not contribute to formal diagnostic criteria:

  • Hyperechoic central stroma
  • Peripheral location of follicles (string of pearls sign)
  • Follicles of similar size measuring 2-9 mm

Few points to remember about Meningioma

  • Location: Meningiomas commonly occur at the brain convexity, parasagittal region, skull base, tentorium, olfactory groove, and sellar/suprasellar areas and CP angle region
  • Shape: Typically well-circumscribed, with a rounded or lobulated appearance.

  • Dural Tail Sign: Tapered enhancement extending along the adjacent dura mater.
  • Calcifications: May exhibit calcifications, visible on CT scans.
  • Meningeal Attachment: Often connected to the dura, showing dural tail sign.

Hyperostosis: Adjacent hyperostosis (thickening of the skull) may be visible on imaging.

  • Transosseous Extension: Meningiomas can extend through bone, leading to extracranial manifestations.
  • Subtypes: Varied histological subtypes exist, influencing imaging characteristics (e.g., psammomatous meningiomas with calcifications).
  • Edema: Peritumoral edema may be present, contributing to mass effect on surrounding structures.
  • Blood Supply: Blood supply often involves branches of the external carotid artery.

question_text: Identify the marked structure given in the image?
explanation:
A, Axial T2-weighted image shows the postcommissural fibers of the fornix (yellow arrows) coursing posterior to the anterior commissure (green arrow). B, Coronal T2-weighted image shows the superoinferior orientation of the columns of the fornix (yellow arrows).

Schematic overview of the fornix from the side. The fimbria forms the crus of the fornix, which is joined to the opposite fornix across the midline by the commissure of the fornix (hippocampal commissure, psalterium). The body of the fornix (B) at the top of the fornical arch is connected to the inferior surface of the body of the corpus callosum by the septum pellucidum. The column of the fornix (C) has a more superoinferior orientation and is connected to the posterior margin of the genu of the corpus callosum by the septum pellucidum. The columns of the fornix are split at the level of the anterior commissure with most the fibers (postcommissural fibers) projecting to the mammillary bodies

Incorrect Choices Explanation

  • Choice A: Pineal Gland
    • The pineal gland is a small, midline endocrine gland located posterior to the third ventricle, near the superior colliculus.
    • It is not associated with the fornix fibers or anterior commissure, making this choice incorrect.
  • Choice C: Pituitary
    • The pituitary gland is located at the base of the brain, within the sella turcica.
    • It is anterior and inferior to the fornix and does not share its distinctive fiber tract appearance.
  • Choice D: Third Ventricle
    • The third ventricle is a CSF-filled space located between the two halves of the diencephalon.
    • While it is anatomically close to the fornix, it is not a fiber tract and would appear differently on MRI.

Key takeaway:

MRI brain anatomy in axial section is must know topic.

Reference:

Raslau, Flavius & Augustinack, Jean & Klein, Andrew & Ulmer, J & Mathews, V & Mark, L. (2015). Memory Part 3: The Role of the Fornix and Clinical Cases. AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology. 36. 10.3174/ajnr.A4371.

question_text: Best diagnostic modality to diagnose avascular necrosis is: March 2007

A: MRI Scan Avascular necrosis/ osteonecrosis/ aseptic (bone) necrosis/ ischemic bone necrosis is a disease resulting from the temporary or permanent loss of the blood supply to the bones. Without blood, the bone tissue dies and causes the bone to collapse. There are many causes of avascular necrosis such as: Alcoholism Excessive steroid use Post trauma Caisson disease (decompression sickness) Vascular compression Vasculitis Thrombosis Damage from radiation Bisphosphonates (particularly the mandible) Sickle cell anaemia Gaucher's Disease Idiopathic (no cause is found). Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus are also common causes of AVN. Avascular necrosis most commonly affects the head of femur. Other Avascular necrosis most commonly affects the head of femur. Other common sites include the talus, scaphoid and the jaw. Avascular necrosis usually affects people between 30 and 50 years of age. When it occurs in children at the femoral head, it is known as Legg- Calve-Perthes syndrome. It is most oftenly diagnose clinically. Because early X-rays are usually normal in the early stage of the disease, bone scintigraphy and MRI are the diagnostic modality of choice since both can detect minimal changes at early stages of the disease. question_text: A 55-year-old man reports multiple episodes of lightheadedness while buttoning a tight shirt collar. During 2 episodes, he passed out briefly but sustained no injuries. His blood pressure was 70/40 mm Hg and pulse was 45/min during one of the episodes. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 125/72 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min without orthostatic changes. Stimulation of afferent sensory fibers in which of the following nerves is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
The patient's history is suggestive of carotid sinus hypersensitivity, triggered by pressure on the carotid sinus by a tight shirt collar. The carotid sinus baroreceptors are important in blood pressure control and use the arterial wall stretch as an indicator of systemic blood pressure.

The carotid sinus is a dilation of the internal carotid artery, located just above the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. The carotid sinus reflex has an afferent limb that arises from the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and travels to the medullary centers via the Hering nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). The efferent limb of the carotid sinus carries parasympathetic impulses via the vagus nerve (CN X). Carotid sinus pressure or massage stimulates the baroreceptors and increases the firing rate from the carotid sinus, leading to an increase in parasympathetic output and withdrawal of sympathetic output to the heart and peripheral vasculature. The result is decreased blood pressure (via peripheral vasodilation) and decreased cardiac output (decreased contractility/stroke volume and heart rate). In sensitive individuals, this response can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, and sometimes syncope.

Option A & C: The accessory (CN XI), hypoglossal (CN XII), nerves do not transmit baroreceptor signals. The accessory nerve controls the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, the hypoglossal nerve primarily controls the muscles of the tongue.

Option D: The vagus nerve (CN X) acts as the afferent limb for the nerve fibers originating from the aortic arch baroreceptors and as an efferent limb for the carotid sinus reflex. However, a tight collar would stimulate carotid sinus (not aortic arch) baroreceptor afferents carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition, Page Number-221.

question_text: A patient presented with hypermobility of the arms. On examination he had a large forehead and highly arched palate. An Xray is done which is shown in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

X-ray shows complete absence of clavicles suggestive of cleidocranial dysplasia

Cleidocranial dysostosis (CCD), also known as cleidocranial dysplasia, is a rare skeletal dysplasia characterized by abnormal development of membranous bones.

It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

Plain Radiograph

  • Multiple Wormian Bones: Extra bones within the sutures of the skull.
  • Widened Sagittal Sutures and/or Fontanelles: Indicating delayed ossification.
  • Premature Fusion of the Coronal Suture: Can lead to brachycephaly (broad, short skull).
  • Frontal and/or Parietal Bossing: Prominent forehead or parietal regions.
  • Basilar Invagination: Potential for atlantoaxial impaction.
  • Persistent Metopic Suture
  • Supernumerary or Abnormal Teeth: Commonly observed in CCD.

KEY TAKE AWAY:

Radiological findings of Cleidocranial dysplasia

Acromegaly (Choice A): Thickened calvarium, enlarged sella turcica, and prognathism; clavicles normal.

Marfan's Syndrome (Choice C): Elongated bones and scoliosis; no clavicular defects.

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Choice D): Soft tissue disorder; radiographs usually normal.

question_text: A patient presented with headaches and hearing loss. He was advised to undergo a skull x-ray which is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The above x-ray shows cotton wool appearance of skull

Paget disease of the bone is a common, chronic bone disorder characterized by excessive abnormal bone remodelling.

The classically described radiological appearances are expanded bone with a coarsened trabecular pattern. The pelvis, spine, skull, and proximal long bones are most frequently affected.

Plain radiographic features will depend upon the phase of the disease.

The early phase features osteolytic (lucent) regions which are later followed by coarsened trabeculae and bony enlargement. Sclerotic changes occur much later in the disease process.

SKULL

  • osteoporosis circumscripta: large, well-defined lytic lesions involving the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull (stage one) with a preserved inner table.
  • cotton wool appearance: mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions of the skull.
  • diploic widening
  • Tam o' Shatner sign: platybasia and basilar invagination with the appearance of the skull falling over the facial bones, like a Tam o' Shatner hat

Spine

  • picture frame sign: Paget disease of the spine frequently manifests with cortical thickening and sclerosis encasing the vertebral margins, which gives rise to this appearance on radiographs in mixed-phase disease
  • IVORY VERTEBRA

Pelvis

  • cortical thickening and sclerosis of the iliopectineal and ischiopubic lines results in the pelvic brim sign and leads to obliteration of Köhler's teardrop
  • acetabular protrusion
  • enlargement of the pubic rami and ischium

These findings are often asymmetric, and for some reason, are more commonly seen on the right side.

Long bones

  • blade of grass or candle flame sign: begins as a subchondral area of lucency with advancing tip of V-shaped osteolysis, extending towards the diaphysis
  • lateral curvature (bowing) of the femur
  • anterior curvature of the tibia

Reference: AIIMS-MAMC-PGI's Comprehensive textbook of diagnostic radiology page no 2743

question_text: A 13-year-old boy presents with restricted abduction and internal rotation of the left hip. The X-ray image of his left hip joint is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) is a disorder of adolescence in which the growth plate (physis) is weakened, allowing the femoral head to slip posteroinferiorly relative to the femoral neck.
It commonly presents as a non-traumatic, painful hip with limited internal rotation and abduction.

Diagnostic imaging:

  • X-ray views: Anteroposterior (AP) pelvis and frog-leg lateral
  • Frog-leg lateral view procedure:
    • Patient supine; hip flexed 30-40° and abducted 45°.
    • Beam centered midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis.
    • For bilateral studies, both knees rest on sponges ("frog-leg" position).

The frog-leg lateral view clearly demonstrates the posterior and inferior displacement of the epiphysis from the metaphysis.

Explanation of other options:

Perthes disease (Option B): Avascular necrosis of the femoral head due to temporary interruption of blood supply. Early signs include joint effusion and widened medial joint space; later stages show femoral head deformity.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (Option C): Abnormal acetabular formation with or without dislocation, present from birth or early infancy. May cause hip instability or dysplasia at skeletal maturity.

Ankylosing spondylitis (Option D): Chronic inflammatory disease of the spine and sacroiliac joints. Radiographically, there is fusion of sacroiliac joints and thin, symmetrical syndesmophytes bridging intervertebral spaces ("bamboo spine").

Key Takeaways:

  • SCFE = posterior/inferior slip of femoral head in adolescents.
  • Frog-leg lateral view is diagnostic.
  • Common in obese adolescent boys.

question_text: A 50-year-old male presents with a right-sided neck swelling, which is pulsatile in nature and is compressible, refilling on removal of pressure. A CT-angiogram was performed and is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of clinical findings (a pulsatile, compressible neck mass) and the pathognomonic imaging feature is diagnostic of a carotid body tumor. This is a type of paraganglioma, a rare and typically benign neuroendocrine tumor arising from the chemoreceptor cells of the carotid body.

Carotid body tumour:

It arises from the carotid body at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery.

  • Clinical features: Presents as a pulsatile, compressible neck swelling, often with bruit/thrill. The tumor can be moved side to side but not up and down, due to its location within the carotid sheath (Fontaine's sign)
  • Common Associations:
    • Seen in familial paraganglioma syndromes (SDH gene mutations).
    • Syndromic association: Can occur in MEN-2, Von Hippel-Lindau disease, NF type 1.
    • High altitude: D/t chronic hypoxia stimulating the carotid body.
  • CT-angiogram: Shows the classic "lyre sign" - splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries by an enhancing mass.
  • MRI: Demonstrates the "salt and pepper appearance" (salt = hyperintense foci from slow flow/hemorrhage; pepper = flow voids from high vascularity).
  • Management: Surgical excision (with or without preoperative embolization). Biopsy is contraindicated due to high risk of bleeding.

Explanation of Other Options:

Carotid aneurysm (Option B): This would appear as a saccular or fusiform dilation of the carotid artery itself on angiography, not as a distinct solid tumor splaying the bifurcation.

AV fistula (Option C): Usually post-traumatic or iatrogenic; causes a continuous bruit/thrill with imaging showing a direct arterial-venous communication. On angiography, it would be characterized by very early and dense filling of veins during the arterial phase, not a well-defined tumor mass.

Hemangioma (Option D): Benign vascular tumor, usually cutaneous/subcutaneous, more common in children, not classically located at the carotid bifurcation.

question_text: The white arrow on the provided MRI of the knee joint points to which structure?
option_b: Lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle
explanation:
• The image is a sagittal view of the knee joint. The arrow points to the large, dark (low signal intensity) tendinous structure located anteriorly, running from the inferior pole of the patella (the large bone superior to the arrow) down to the tibial tuberosity (just out of frame inferiorly).
  • Anatomical Identification: This location and appearance are characteristic of the patellar tendon (also known as the patellar ligament). It is the continuation of the quadriceps tendon and is crucial for knee extension.

Explanation of Other Options:

Popliteus tendon (Option A): The popliteus tendon is located on the posterior and lateral aspect of the knee joint and would be seen behind the femoral and tibial condyles in a sagittal view.

Lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle (Option B): This large muscle is located on the posterior aspect of the knee and forms the calf.

Tibialis anterior muscle (Option D): This muscle is located further distally on the anterior aspect of the lower leg; it does not attach to the patella.

Key Takeaways:

On a sagittal MRI of the knee, it is crucial to identify the major anterior structures:

  • The largest muscle superiorly is the quadriceps.
  • The bone within its tendon is the patella.
  • The thick tendon extending inferiorly from the patella to the tibia is the patellar tendon.

Reference:

Musculoskeletal MRI, 2nd Edition, Page Number: 375.

question_text: Head Cheese Sign is seen in?
explanation:
The "head cheese sign" refers to a radiological finding seen in hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), a condition characterized by inflammation of the lung tissue due to an allergic response to inhaled organic dusts.

The head cheese sign is described as a pattern of alternating areas of ground glass opacities (GGO) and areas of normal lung tissue, resembling the appearance of head cheese, a type of meat product with a mottled or marbled appearance. This pattern is also known as the "mosaic attenuation pattern" due to its appearance on imaging.

The presence of the head cheese sign on imaging can be suggestive of HP.

question_text: A patient presented with loss of coordination, difficulty in speech and vertigo. He also complains of visual disturbances, headache and palpitations. On doing an MRI, a space occupying lesion is noted in the cerebellum as shown below. What would be the expected finding in the kidneys?
explanation:
Explanation:

The cerebellar mass described is most consistent with a hemangioblastoma, a characteristic CNS tumor associated with Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease. VHL is an autosomal dominant hereditary syndrome that predisposes individuals to multiple tumors and cysts in various organs.

Renal involvement in VHL most commonly includes:

  • Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC) – the most frequent malignant tumor associated with VHL
  • Often bilateral and multifocal
  • Occurs in >67% of VHL patients

Other VHL-associated renal findings include:

  • Renal cysts (simple or complex), present in ~75%
  • Potential for cystic RCC
  • Renal angiomyolipomas (benign)

Systemic Tumor Spectrum in VHL:

Adrenal:

  • Pheochromocytomas:Found in 25-30% of patients. Accounts for palpitations and headache in the history given above. other important features are episodic hypertension and orthostatic hypotension.
  • Extra-adrenal Pheochromocytomas/Paragangliomas

Pancreas:

  • Pancreatic Cysts:Approximately 40% of patients may have these.
  • Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (pNET)
  • Pancreatic Serous Cystadenomas

Urogenital System:

  • Epididymal Cysts: Present in many patients.
  • Papillary Cystadenoma of the Epididymis
  • Broad Ligament Cystadenomas.

Central Nervous System (CNS):

  • CNS Hemangioblastomas: Found in about 70% of patients. Commonly located in the cerebellum (60%) and spinal cord (30%), particularly cervical and thoracic regions.
  • Choroid Plexus Papilloma: May occur.

Head and Neck:

  • Retinal Hemangioblastomas: The most common presenting feature, seen in 45-60% of patients, can lead to vision loss.
  • Endolymphatic Sac Tumors (ELST): Present in 10-15% of patients and bilateral in 30%, considered pathognomonic for vHL.

Urate renal calculi (Option A): Seen in gout or tumor lysis syndrome, not associated with VHL.

Complex renal cysts (Option C): Though cysts may occur in VHL, the question asks for the expected pathological lesion associated with the cerebellar mass; thus, clear cell carcinoma is more specific.

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (Option D): Associated with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, not VHL.

Key Takeaway:

question_text: The incision preferred during an autopsy in case of asphyxial death due to neck compression is:
explanation:
• The incision preferred in a case of asphyxial death due to neck compression (as in hanging, strangulation etc.) is the Y-shaped incision.
  1. I-shaped incision: The incision is drawn from just below the chin to the pubic symphysis avoiding the umbilicus and any injuries along the line of incision. This is the most common method followed.
  2. Y-shaped incision: The two incisions are made which commence on either side of the neck from 2 to 3 cm behind the lobe of each ear to meet at manubrium sterni, and then continue as a single incision down to the pubic symphysis, avoiding the umbilicus. It is used when a detailed study of the neck organs is required, such as death due to compression on the neck (hanging or strangulation) and any condition where the larynx might be damaged, as the skin of the upper neck can then be dissected off the mandible and raised to give a wide approach to the neck structures.
  3. Modified Y-shaped incision: Two incisions are made, commencing on either side of the chest starting from both the acromia, running away and below the breasts to meet at the xiphisternum and to be continued as a single vertical incision down to the pubic symphysis, avoiding the umbilicus. This is desirable in those cases (especially females) where it is customary to restore the body in a reasonable cosmetic condition for viewing sometime after death.
  4. Inverted Y- shaped incision: An incision from the symphysis menti to umbilicus, then extending to bilateral mid-inguinal point. It is used in fetuses and newborns to study the umbilical arteries.

References: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology by Kishan Vij, 5th Edition, Page Number-20; Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page Number-19.

Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous

question_text: A neonate presents with signs of high-output cardiac failure and a prominent cranial bruit. A sagittal CT angiogram of the head is performed, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Image Findings: The sagittal CT angiogram demonstrates a large, midline, aneurysmal dilatation of a deep cerebral vein, consistent with a markedly enlarged vein of Galen. This is the pathognomonic radiological finding.
  • Clinical Correlation: The patient's presentation with high-output cardiac failure in infancy is the classic clinical scenario for a Vein of Galen Malformation (VOGM).
  • Pathophysiology: A VOGM is not a true aneurysm but a rare arteriovenous malformation (AVM) where choroidal arteries connect directly to the embryonic median prosencephalic vein (a precursor to the vein of Galen). This massive, low-resistance arteriovenous shunt diverts a large portion of the cardiac output, leading to high-output heart failure.

Explanation of Other Options:

Dandy-Walker Malformation (Option A): This is a congenital malformation of the posterior fossa characterized by agenesis of the cerebellar vermis and cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle. It would not appear as a large vascular structure on angiography.

Chiari Malformation (Option B): This is a structural defect characterized by the downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum. It is a structural, not vascular, anomaly.

Tuberculous Meningitis (Option D): Tuberculous meningitis is an infection that would typically show signs of basilar meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, or infarcts on imaging, not a large AVM.

Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8719232/

question_text: Identify the type of fracture shown below

• Neck of femur fractures (NOF), a.k.a. femoral neck fractures, are common injuries sustained by older patients who are both more likely to have unsteadiness of gait and reduced bone mineral density, predisposing to fracture.
  • Elderly osteoporotic women are at greatest risk. Since disruption of blood supply to the femoral head is dependent on the type of fracture and causes significant morbidity, the diagnosis and classification of these fractures is important. There are three types:

Sub capital and transcervical fractures are considered intracapsular fractures.

A feeding artery and a well-defined nidus are characteristic features of an arteriovenous malformation (AVM). AVMs are abnormal tangles of blood vessels where arteries connect directly to veins without the usual capillary network between them. This abnormal connection of blood vessels can lead to various symptoms, depending on the location and size of the AVM, and may require treatment to prevent complications such as bleeding or neurological deficits.

question_text: A 45 year old male presented with backache since 20 years and difficulty during neck movements. Most likely diagnosis based on this cervical spine radiograph is?
explanation:
DISH, often referred to as Forestier disease, is a common disorder found in the late middle aged/ elderly with an unknown etiology. It is characterized by marked hyperosteosis seen at multiple sites, but classically involving the spine. There is multilevel spinal involvement with flowing ligamentous ossifications.

The diagnostic criteria for DISH are:

  • Presence of ossification along the anterolateral aspect of at least four contiguous vertebral bodies.
  • Preserved disc height
  • Absence of facet joint ankylosis or SI joint fusion.
