question_text: Which of the following bone is not a common site of avascular necrosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neck of humerus fracture is not a typical location of avascular necrosis

Osteonecrosis is a generic term referring to the ischemic death of the constituents of bone. It has a wide variety of causes and can affect nearly any bone in the body.

KEY TAKE AWAY:

Classification by eponymous names

  • Buchman Disease: Iliac crest
  • Burns Disease: Distal ulna
  • Freiberg Infraction: Head of the second metatarsal
  • Friedrich Disease: Medial clavicle
  • Haas Disease: Humeral head
  • Kienbock Disease: Lunate
  • Kohler Disease: Patella or navicular (children)
  • Kummell Disease: Vertebral body
  • Legg-Calve-Perthes Disease: Femoral head
  • Panner Disease: Capitellum of the humerus
  • Pierson Disease: Symphysis pubis
  • Preiser Disease: Scaphoid
  • Sever Disease: Calcaneal epiphysis

Scaphoid (Option A):

Prone to AVN of its proximal pole due to retrograde blood supply from the radial artery - disrupted in fractures through the waist.

Talus (Option B):

One of the most common sites of AVN because most of its surface is covered by cartilage, leaving limited vascular entry points, which are easily disrupted by trauma.

Head of femur (Option D):

Classic and most frequent site of AVN, particularly after neck of femur fracture or steroid use, as the retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head are easily compromised.

question_text: A child presented with hip pain since 3 months. He underwent an x-ray which is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE), also known as a slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), is a relatively common condition affecting the physis of the proximal femur in adolescents.
  • Slipped upper femoral epiphysis is more common in boys than girls. Obesity is a significant risk factor.

The radiographic features include:

  • Widening of the metaphysis and displacement
  • On the AP, a line drawn up the lateral edge of the femoral neck (line of Klein) fails to intersect the epiphysis during the acute phase (Trethowan's).

question_text: A patient presented with a head injury after a hammer fell on the skull. His CT is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Depressed Skull Fracture:

This fracture occurs when a portion of the skull is driven inward, potentially compressing or injuring the underlying brain tissue.

  • CT findings: Imaging shows bone fragments displaced beneath the normal skull contour, appearing as an indentation.
  • Such fractures are typically the result of a direct blow to the head with a heavy object (e.g., a hammer).
  • Clinical features: Patients may present with localized pain, swelling, and, in some cases, neurological deficits if brain tissue is affected.

Explanation of other options:

Concussion (Option A) is a functional brain injury without structural abnormalities visible on CT. It results from head trauma and commonly presents with transient confusion, headache, or brief loss of consciousness.

Epidural Hematoma (Option B): On CT, an epidural hematoma appears as a biconvex, hyperdense collection between the skull and dura. It is usually linked to a temporal bone fracture, not depressed skull fragments.

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (Option D: This condition shows blood within the subarachnoid spaces (such as sulci or cisterns) on CT. It is most often due to trauma or rupture of an aneurysm, rather than a depressed skull fracture.

question_text: A 30 year old male presents with sudden onset of high fever, headache, confusion and seizures, MRI shows hyperintensities in bilateral temporal lobes, probable diagnosis is?
explanation: The clinical presentation of sudden onset fever, headache, confusion, and seizures, along with MRI findings of hyperintensities in bilateral temporal lobes, is highly suggestive of herpes encephalitis. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a common cause of viral encephalitis and often presents with these characteristic symptoms and imaging findings. Other infections such as tuberculosis, neurocysticercosis, and toxoplasmosis may present with similar symptoms but typically have different imaging findings and clinical features.

chest

pelvis

  • coxa vara

general

  • Mother in Law Sign
  • Skeletal Hyperostosis
  • Pneumosinus Dilatans
  • Spoke wheel Pattern/Sunray appearance Of vasculature

Common Radiological Sites:

  • Convexity: Along the outer layer of the dura mater on the cerebral hemispheres.
  • Parasagittal: Adjacent to the superior sagittal sinus.
  • Sphenoid wing: Involving the sphenoid bone, often impacting the cavernous sinus.
  • Olfactory groove: Near the olfactory bulb in the frontal lobe region.
  • Posterior fossa: Around the cerebellum or brainstem.

Radiological Features:

  • Extra-axial masses with well-defined margins.
  • Iso- to hypointense signals on T1-weighted MRI images.
  • Iso- to hyperintense signals on T2-weighted MRI images.
  • Avid contrast enhancement with dural tail sign.
  • Hyperdense lesions with calcifications may be visible on CT scans.

Note: Biopsy for histopathological examination is essential for a definitive diagnosis. Early detection and treatment are crucial for optimal outcomes.

Medulloblastoma is a highly malignant brain tumor primarily affecting children. Radiologically, it typically presents as a midline mass in the posterior fossa on MRI, often with associated hydrocephalus due to obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow. CT scans may show a hyperdense lesion with surrounding edema. Enhancements post-contrast administration and presence of calcifications are common features. However, definitive diagnosis requires histopathological examination via biopsy.

question_text:
An HIV patient presents with Headache and Altered sensorium. Consider the following evidences about his condition. Which of these is an Absolute Criteria for diagnosis of NCC?
1. Brain biopsy shows Taenia solium
2. MRI brain shows the typical cyst-with-a-dot sign
3. CT showing ventriculomegaly with multiple periventricular calcifications
4. Muscle showing multiple focal calcifications
explanation:
Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is caused by the Taenia solium larvae infecting the central nervous system (CNS). The absolute criteria for diagnosing NCC include:

  • Brain biopsy showing Taenia solium → Absolute criterion
    • Direct visualization of the parasite in tissue confirms the diagnosis.
  • MRI brain shows the typical cyst-with-a-dot sign → Absolute criterion
    • This classic imaging feature represents the scolex within the cyst and is highly specific for NCC.
  • CT showing ventriculomegaly with multiple periventricular calcifications
    • This is a supportive finding but not an absolute criterion. Other conditions (e.g., tuberculosis, CMV, or other infections) can also cause similar findings.
  • Muscle showing multiple focal calcifications
    • This suggests systemic cysticercosis but does not confirm neurocysticercosis specifically.

Absolute Criteria for NCC Diagnosis (Del Brutto’s Criteria):

According to Del Brutto's diagnostic criteria, the absolute criteria are:

  • Histological confirmation of the parasite (biopsy).
  • Imaging showing a cystic lesion with a scolex (cyst-with-dot sign).
  • Direct visualization of the parasite in the eye (ophthalmoscopy).

question_text: A 50-year-old male, who is a known case of PLHA, has had complaints of headache and dizziness for 2 days. Which of the following cells in the brain are predominantly infected by HIV?

The clinical syndrome of CNS abnormalities is called HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND). Microglia, cells in the CNS that belong to the macrophage lineage, are the predominant cell types in the brain that are infected with HIV. It is believed that HIV is carried into the brain by infected T cells or monocytes. The mechanism of HIV-induced damage of the brain remains obscure. Because neurons are not infected by HIV and the extent of neuropathologic changes is less than expected from the severity of neurologic symptoms, most workers believe that the neurologic deficit is caused indirectly by viral products and by soluble factors produced by infected microglia.

question_text: The sequential onset of rigor mortis is described by which of the following?
explanation:
• Nysten's rule describes the sequential onset of rigor mortis in the various muscle groups.
  • Rigor mortis (cadaveric rigidity or death stiffening) refers to the stiffening and shortening of muscles following death. The basic sequence of the rigor mortis begins from the head and continues downwards the body. It disappears in the same order of appearance.
  • Heart (left chamber of the heart is affected first) is the first organ to undergo rigor mortis.

Externally, the muscles are affected in following order:

  1. Eyelids
  2. Neck & lower jaw
  3. Face
  4. Chest
  5. Upper limbs
  6. Abdomen
  7. Lower limbs
  8. Fingers & toes

Puppe's rule: Helps in determining the sequence of bullets hitting the skull, when there are multiple bullet injuries to the skull. The fracture line resulting from the later bullet will typically stop at the previously formed one.

Casper's dictum: It is used in the estimation of time since death. It states that a body decomposes in air twice as rapidly as in water (immersed body), and eight times as rapidly as in earth (buried body), if the environmental factors are the same. Air: Water: Earth → 1: 2: 8.

Durham's rule: An accused is not criminally responsible if his unlawful act is the product of a mental disease or a mental defect.

question_text: A young adolescent boy presented with history of pain and limping in the lower limbs. On examination he was found to have grade I obesity. An Xray was done. What is the expected finding in this case?

Explanation:

Perthes Disease (Legg-Calve-Perthes Disease)

Perthes disease is an idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head in children. It's crucial to diagnose it as a condition of exclusion, ruling out other causes of osteonecrosis such as sickle cell disease, leukemia, corticosteroid use, and Gaucher disease.

Clinical Presentation

  • Common symptoms include atraumatic hip pain and limp.
  • Some children may have a history of minor trauma, but this is not always present.

Radiographic Findings

The disease is characterized by specific radiographic stages that reflect the severity of osteonecrosis and the duration of compromised blood supply:

Early Stage

  • No appreciable changes may be seen.
  • Joint effusion: Widening of the medial joint space.
  • Asymmetrical femoral epiphyseal size: The affected side may appear smaller.
  • Increased density of the femoral head epiphysis.
  • Blurring of the physeal plate.
  • Radiolucency of the proximal metaphysis.

Established Stage

  • Reduction in epiphyseal size and lucency in the femoral head.
  • Fragmentation and destruction of the femoral head may begin (Stage 2).

Late Stage (Burnt-Out Stage)

  • Deformity of the femoral head: Widening and flattening (known as coxa plana).
  • Proximal femoral neck deformity: Development of coxa magna.
  • 'Sagging rope sign': A thin sclerotic line across the femoral neck.
  • Possible lucencies extending inferolaterally into the femoral neck, which must be differentiated from infections or neoplasms.

Key MRI features to assess include:

  1. Deformity of the femoral head.
  2. Congruence: How well the femoral head fits within the acetabulum.
  3. Containment: The degree of lateral subluxation of the flattened femoral head.

Severe cases may lead to hinge abduction, where the femoral head pivots on the lateral acetabular rim rather than moving medially during hip abduction.

Nuclear Medicine

  • Bone Scintigraphy: Early stages may show reduced uptake in the femoral head due to decreased blood supply. In later stages, increased uptake may indicate repair processes and degenerative changes.

KEY TAKE AWAY:

question_text: Trethowan sign is used in radiological diagnosis of?
option_d: Avascular Necrosis of head of femur Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
explanation:
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) is a hip disorder that primarily affects adolescents during their growth spurt. In SCFE, the femoral head (ball of the hip joint) slips off the neck of the femur at the epiphyseal plate. Radiological imaging plays a crucial role in diagnosing and assessing SCFE. Here are the typical radiological findings associated with SCFE:

Posteroinferior Slip: SCFE usually involves a posteroinferior slip of the femoral epiphysis. On an anteroposterior (AP) pelvic radiograph, the affected hip may demonstrate the classic appearance of the femoral head being displaced posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the femoral neck.

Widening of the Growth Plate: Radiographs often reveal widening of the growth plate at the epiphysis, which is a key indicator of SCFE. This widening is due to the displacement of the femoral head from the femoral neck.

Shear or Crescent Sign: The "shear" or "crescent" sign is a radiological finding seen on the frog-leg lateral view. It represents the separation of the femoral epiphysis from the metaphysis, creating a radiolucent line or crescent.

Klein's Line: Klein's line is a reference line drawn along the superior margin of the femoral neck on an AP radiograph. In SCFE, the femoral head may not intersect or be superior to Klein's line, indicating slippage.

Decreased Neck-Shaft Angle: SCFE can result in a decreased neck-shaft angle on an AP radiograph. This change is due to the displacement of the femoral head, leading to an altered geometry of the hip joint.

Obligatory External Rotation: The affected leg may appear externally rotated, especially when compared to the contralateral side. This finding may be evident on clinical examination and can be confirmed radiographically.

Pistol Grip Deformity: Over time, SCFE may lead to changes in the shape of the femoral head, resulting in a "pistol grip" deformity. This can be seen on radiographs and indicates ongoing structural changes in the hip joint.

It's important to note that early diagnosis and prompt management of SCFE are crucial to prevent further slippage and complications. Once SCFE is suspected clinically, imaging studies, particularly hip radiographs (AP and frog-leg lateral views), are typically obtained to confirm the diagnosis and assess the severity of the slip. Surgical intervention is often required to stabilize the hip joint and prevent further slippage.

Trethowan's sign is normally used for diagnosis of a slip in slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

Normally on AP view of hip a line drawn along the superior surface of the neck of the femur passes through a third of the head (klein line)whereas in a slipped epiphysis the line passes superior to the head

question_text: A child with no history of fever presents with the following findings. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows the characteristic "cobra-head" appearance, which is a feature of ureterocoele.

Ureterocele

Definition: A ureterocele is a submucosal cystic dilatation of the distal intramural ureter, often projecting into the bladder lumen.

Epidemiology

  • Female: Male ratio ≈ 4:1
  • Most commonly associated with the upper moiety ureter of a duplex system → usually ectopic
  • Minority: not associated with duplication → often present in adults, usually small, sometimes incidental finding

Clinical Features

  • Children (ectopic ureterocele) → Often symptomatic with obstruction, hydroureteronephrosis, recurrent UTIs
  • May obstruct other ureter in duplex system or urethral orifice, causing bilateral hydronephrosis
  • Adults (non-duplicated ureterocele) → Often incidental, small; may present with calculi, recurrent UTI; rarely cause significant obstruction unless complicated by stone

Imaging Features

  • Intravenous Urography (IVU): Contrast-filled sac in bladder with thin, smooth radiolucent wall. Surrounded by bladder contrast → "Cobra head sign." If associated kidney is non-functioning → appears as well-defined radiolucent mass in bladder.

  • Ultrasound: Thin-walled, cystic structure projecting into bladder lumen at ureteric insertion. May show associated ureteric calculi, hydroureter, hydronephrosis.

Posterior urethral valves (PUV) (Option B): Occurs only in boys, causes bladder outlet obstruction, recurrent UTIs/fever, poor stream, and shows a dilated posterior urethra on MCU-not a cystic lesion at the ureteric orifice.

Bladder diverticulum (Option C): An outpouching through the bladder wall that communicates via a neck; it does not arise from the ureteric orifice and lacks the cobra-head appearance. It's an extravesical sac, not a submucosal intramural ureter dilation.

Ectopic ureter (Option D): Typically presents (especially in girls) with continuous dribbling/incontinence despite normal voiding; imaging shows an abnormally located ureteric orifice (outside the trigone), not an intravesical cystic sac.

question_text: A young infant was brought to OPD with history of fall. He was irritable on examination. On doing an examination multiple bruises were found. On doing a skeletal survey the following image was obtained. What is the diagnosis

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a group of congenital, non-sex-linked genetic disorders characterized by defective production of collagen type I.

This condition primarily affects connective tissues and bones, leading to notable clinical features.

Key Features

  • Osteoporosis and Fragility
  • Blue Sclera: A distinct bluish tint to the sclera due to reduced collagen.
  • Dental Fragility
  • Hearing Loss: Often due to inner ear abnormalities.

Plain radiography is the initial examination of choice for assessing OI. Key findings include:

Head, Neck, and Spine:

  • Basilar Invagination
  • Wormian Bones
  • Kyphoscoliosis
  • Vertebral Compression Fractures
  • Codfish Vertebrae
  • Platyspondyly

Chest:

  • Pectus Excavatum or Carinatum
  • Accordion Ribs: Ribs appear narrow and angled.

Pelvis:

  • Protrusio Acetabuli
  • Coxa Vara

General Findings:

  • Severe Osteoporosis
  • Deformed, Gracile Bones
  • Cortical Thinning
  • Hyperplastic Callus Formation
  • Popcorn Calcification: Scalloped radiolucent areas in metaphysis and epiphysis with sclerotic margins.
  • Zebra Stripe Sign: Sclerotic lines in long bones due to bisphosphonate treatment.
  • Pseudarthrosis Formation

KEY TAKE AWAY:

Perthe's Disease (Choice A): Localized avascular necrosis of femoral head; no generalized osteopenia or multiple fractures.

Achondroplasia (Choice B): Shows rhizomelic limb shortening with normal bone density and no fractures.

Acromegaly (Choice C): Characterized by thickened bones and enlarged sinuses, not bone

question_text: An elderly hypertensive patient came with a history of fall, following which he is confused, lethargic, disoriented and unable to speak properly. He was advised to undergo a CT scan of the head which is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given non-contrast CT image shows a crescent-shaped, hyperdense extra-axial collection along the cerebral convexity. The collection extends across sutures but does not cross the midline due to the falx cerebri barrier. This appearance is characteristic of a subdural hemorrhage (SDH). The density suggests acute blood, and the mass effect with compression of adjacent sulci or midline shift may be evident.

Subdural hemorrhage commonly results from rupture of bridging veins, particularly in elderly or atrophic brains where the veins are stretched and more vulnerable to trauma, even from minor falls.


Extradural Hemorrhage (Option B): An extradural (epidural) hemorrhage appears as a biconvex or lentiform hyperdense collection limited by cranial sutures, usually located adjacent to a skull fracture and caused by arterial injury, most commonly the middle meningeal artery. It typically does not cross suture lines and has sharply defined margins. The absence of a lentiform configuration and the presence of a crescentic shape rule out an extradural bleed in this case.

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (Option C): A subarachnoid hemorrhage manifests as hyperdense blood within the basal cisterns, sulci, or fissures, rather than as an extra-axial convexity collection. The blood conforms to the contours of the brain surface and cisternal spaces, not the crescentic extra-axial pattern seen here. Hence, the imaging appearance is inconsistent with subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Intraparenchymal Hemorrhage (Option D): Intraparenchymal hemorrhage presents as a well-defined hyperdense focus within the brain parenchyma, often surrounded by vasogenic edema and causing localized mass effect. It does not have the crescentic extra-axial configuration seen in this image. Therefore, intraparenchymal bleed can be excluded.

Key Takeaway:

EDH usually occurs with forceful impact injury, like road traffic accidents in young.

SDH usually occurs with trivial injury seen in elderly population.

question_text: A patient presented with a history of throbbing headache and blurring of vision. On doing a CT scan and angiogram of the brain, the following image was obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a tangle of abnormal, serpiginous vessels (vascular nidus) with early venous drainage on angiography, classic for an intracranial AVM producing throbbing headache and visual symptoms from haemorrhage or venous hypertension.

Brain arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are high-flow vascular malformations characterized by a complex tangle of blood vessels that includes enlarged feeding arteries, a nidus where arteriovenous shunting occurs, and draining veins. They are the most common symptomatic vascular malformations of the brain.

Clinical Presentation:

AVMs can present in various ways:

  • Incidental Finding: Detected in asymptomatic patients (15%).
  • Seizures: Occur in about 20% of patients.
  • Headaches: Common complaint.
  • Focal Neurological Deficits: Observed in approximately 15%.
  • Hemorrhage: The most common presentation, occurring in about 65% of cases, with an annual incidence of 2-3%. Hemorrhage can manifest as:
    • Parenchymal
    • Subarachnoid
    • Intraventricular

Diagnosis:

Non-Contrast CT

  • Appearance: The nidus may be hyperdense compared to adjacent brain tissue, and enlarged draining veins may be visible. However, large AVMs usually do not exert mass effect unless they bleed.

Contrast-Enhanced Imaging

  • CT Angiography (CTA): After contrast administration, the AVM becomes more apparent, revealing the characteristic "bag of worms" appearance with visible feeding arteries, draining veins, and the nidus

Angiography (Digital Subtraction Angiography - DSA)

  • Gold Standard: Cerebral angiography remains the definitive method for evaluating AVMs.

Dural AVF (Option B): Dural fistulae are dural-based shunts draining into a sinus or cortical veins; angiography shows transdural arterial feeders and a dural pouch rather than an intraparenchymal nidus.

Microhemorrhages (Option C): Appear as tiny focal hemorrhages (punctate), not a vascular nidus with early venous filling on angio.

Brain IPH (Option D): Shows a localized hyperdense hematoma on CT without the organized nidus and early draining veins seen on angiography.

question_text: Which nerve is damaged in this fracture?
explanation:
Explanation:

Radial nerve:
Fractures involving the shaft of the humerus often injure the radial nerve because it courses along the spiral (radial) groove of the bone.

Key manifestations of radial nerve injury:

  • Wrist drop from paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors
  • Weak forearm extension due to loss of triceps contribution (if injury is high)
  • Sensory deficit over the dorsum of the hand, most prominent in the first web space

Explanation of other options:

Ulnar nerve (Option B): Commonly compromised in medial epicondyle fractures, not shaft fractures. Injury produces a claw hand with sensory loss over the medial 1½ fingers.

Median nerve (Option C): Typically affected in distal humerus or supracondylar fractures. Results in the hand of benediction along with sensory loss in the lateral 3½ fingers.

Axillary nerve (Option D): Most at risk with surgical neck fractures or shoulder dislocations. Leads to deltoid weakness and loss of sensation in the regimental badge area (lateral shoulder).

question_text: An 8-year-old presents to the orthopedics OPD with complaints of a painless limp for the past 1 week. An X-ray is done and is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This child's age, presentation of painless limp, and X-ray changes are classic for Perthes disease.

Perthes disease (Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease) is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head seen commonly in boys aged 4-10 years.

  • Clinical feature: Painless limp (most common presentation) ± mild hip/knee pain.
  • X-ray findings: Fragmentation, flattening, and sclerosis of femoral head with loss of normal spherical contour.
  • Pathology: Interruption of blood supply → avascular necrosis → collapse and regeneration of femoral head.
  • Complication: Hip deformity and osteoarthritis if untreated.

Explanation of Other Options:

Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) (Option A): This condition typically presents in infancy with hip instability. Clinical signs include limited abduction, leg length discrepancy, positive Barlow/Ortolani tests, not painless limp in an older child. The X-ray findings would be a shallow acetabulum and a superolaterally displaced femoral head, not a fragmented one.

Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) (Option B): It typically affects obese adolescents (10-16 years) and presents with a painful limp. The characteristic X-ray finding is a posteroinferior slip of the femoral epiphysis (described as an "ice cream scoop falling off a cone"), not fragmentation. A key diagnostic sign on an AP X-ray is a positive Trethowan's sign, where Klein's line (drawn along the superior femoral neck) fails to intersect the slipped femoral head.

Tuberculosis Hip (Option D): Presents with painful limp, night cries, fever, weight loss. X-ray shows narrowing of joint space, periarticular osteopenia, and erosions (Phemister’s triad), not fragmentation of femoral head.

question_text: An elderly patient came with a sudden onset of headache and 2 episodes of vomiting. The NCCT head was given. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH):
    • The classical presenting symptom is a sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache, often described as the worst headache of life.
    • It is commonly associated with nausea, projectile vomiting, neck stiffness, and photophobia due to irritation of the meninges by blood.
  • In elderly patients, SAH should be suspected with sudden onset of severe headache and vomiting.
  • NCCT head is the first-line investigation, which can identify bleeding in the subarachnoid space.

Meningococcal meningitis (Option B): Presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered sensorium. Usually subacute in onset, not as sudden and severe as SAH. CT head is often normal unless there are complications.

Brain abscess (Option C): Presents with fever, focal neurological deficits, seizures, and raised ICP symptoms (headache, vomiting). Progresses gradually, unlike the sudden onset seen in SAH.

Pneumocephalus (Option D): It usually occurs after trauma, neurosurgery, or sinus fracture. Presents with headache and sometimes neurologic symptoms, but not the classic sudden severe headache of SAH.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441958/

explanation: The silhouetting sign in chest X-rays (CXR) refers to the loss of the normal border between two adjacent structures of similar density, leading to the inability to differentiate them. The silhouette sign is useful in localizing pathology within the chest and can help differentiate between structures when interpreting a CXR.

question_text: A patient presented with abdominal pain and vomiting. On eliciting further history, it was found that she had a psychiatric illness. On examination, there was evidence of balding on one side of the head. The doctor advised a barium swallow examination, which is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows mottled intragastric filling defect with a smooth outline and interspersed barium streaks, suggestive of intragastric bezoar.

Bezoars are accumulations of indigestible substances within the gastrointestinal tract, often leading to complications such as small bowel obstruction.

  • Common Associations:
    • Previous Gastric Surgery: Patients with a history of gastric surgery are at increased risk.
    • Psychiatric Illness: Certain psychiatric conditions may contribute to the formation of bezoars.

Types of Bezoars:

1. Trichobezoar: Formed from hair. When the tail extends through the small bowel, it is referred to asRapunzel syndrome.

2. Phytobezoar: Composed of indigestible food materials (e.g., cellulose) and commonly seen in patients with impaired digestion or decreased gastric motility.

Bezoars can lead to small bowel obstruction, and imaging, particularly CT, may reveal the following features:

  • Mass Appearance: The bezoar may appear as a mass in the obstructed segment of the bowel.
  • Outlining Fluid: It may be surrounded by fluid in the proximally dilated small bowel.
  • Mottled Appearance: The mass may have a mottled appearance due to trapped air within it.

Stomach carcinoma (Option A): Gastric carcinoma appears on imaging as a mass lesion or irregular mucosal thickening, sometimes producing an "apple core" deformity on barium study. It does not show a well-defined intraluminal filling defect with a smooth outline like a bezoar. Also, there's no history linking it to psychiatric illness or hair ingestion.

Alopecia (Option B): Alopecia refers to hair loss and is not a gastrointestinal condition.

Phytobezoar (Option D): A phytobezoar is a mass of indigestible plant material, commonly formed in patients with gastric motility disorders or previous gastric surgery. On barium study, it appears as a mottled intraluminal filling defect, but the history would typically involve dietary factors, not psychiatric illness or hair ingestion.

question_text: A 55 Year old male with progressive shortness of breath shows traction bronchiectasis, bibasal fibrosis with volume loss of lungs on HRCT, Barium swallow shows dilated patulous esophagus, most likely cause is?
explanation: The combination of findings-progressive shortness of breath, traction bronchiectasis, bibasal fibrosis with volume loss of lungs on HRCT, and dilated patulous esophagus on barium swallow-points towards scleroderma as the most likely cause. Scleroderma, or systemic sclerosis, is a connective tissue disorder characterized by fibrosis and vascular abnormalities. It can affect multiple organs, including the lungs and esophagus, leading to symptoms such as shortness of breath and esophageal dysfunction. Traction bronchiectasis and bibasal fibrosis are common findings in scleroderma-related interstitial lung disease, and esophageal dysmotility can result in a dilated esophagus on imaging.

question_text: Dependant Viscera sign is seen in?

• The "dependent viscera sign" is a radiological finding seen on a chest X-ray or CT scan in cases of diaphragmatic injury. It refers to the abnormal position of abdominal organs (viscera) that have herniated into the chest cavity due to a tear or rupture in the diaphragm. This sign is called "dependent" because the herniated organs appear to depend or hang downward into the chest cavity.
  • Diaphragmatic injuries can occur due to trauma, such as blunt or penetrating trauma to the abdomen or chest. The herniation of abdominal organs into the chest cavity can lead to respiratory symptoms, gastrointestinal symptoms, or even life-threatening complications such as strangulation of the herniated organs.
  • The dependent viscera sign is one of the radiological findings that can suggest the presence of diaphragmatic injury, and it is important for radiologists and clinicians to recognize this sign to guide appropriate management. question_text: A coal worker presented with chronic breathlessness and cough. On doing a CXR, the following image was obtained. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF) represents the advanced stage of pneumoconiosis such as coal worker's pneumoconiosis or silicosis. It is characterized by large mass-like opacities, predominantly in the upper lobes with irregular margins, fibrosis, and surrounding emphysematous changes. The image demonstrates these hallmark features.

PMF results from coalescence of multiple nodules into fibrotic conglomerate masses.

Radiographic Features:

  • Plain Radiograph:
    • Large, symmetric, upper-lobe opacities
    • Irregular margins
    • May migrate toward the hilum
  • CT Scan:
    • Mass-like "sausage-shaped" opacities
    • Radiating fibrotic strands
    • Areas of air bronchograms
    • Possible calcifications

PMF indicates advanced disease with significant respiratory impairment.

Egg shell calcifications (Option A): Seen in lymph nodes in diseases like silicosis, sarcoidosis, histoplasmosis, and TB.

Round pneumonia (Option B): Appears as a well-circumscribed, solitary opacity, usually in children, without signs of chronic fibrosis.

Alveolar silicoproteinosis (Option D): Acute silicosis with bilateral central consolidation and ground-glass opacities, not large fibrotic masses.

KEY TAKEAWAY:

Progressive Massive Fibrosis occurs in:

  • Silicosis
  • Coal worker's pneumoconiosis
  • Talcosis

question_text: A 1-year-old child presented with complaints of fever and excessive crying while passing urine. He was advised to undergo an USG examination. The duplication of the renal collecting system is indeed the most common congenital urinary tract anomaly, typically arising from the development of two ureteric buds from a single Wolffian duct. This condition results in the formation of an upper and lower renal moiety, each with its own ureter.

  • Ureteric Bud Development: The anomaly occurs when two ureteric buds form from one Wolffian duct, leading to duplicated renal systems.
  • Ureter Insertion:
    • Lower Pole Ureter: Usually inserts normally into the trigone of the bladder, maintaining a standard anatomical position.
    • Upper Pole Ureter: Often has an ectopic insertion, which can occur medially and inferiorly within the bladder, or in some cases, it may insert into the urethra, vagina, or uterus in females, and into the ejaculatory duct in males.

question_text: All are Radiological Features of congenital hypothyroidism except?
explanation:
Radiological features of congenital hypothyroidism include delayed bone age, delayed closure of cranial sutures (not fused sutures - option C) large fontanelle, wormian bones, and epiphyseal dysgenesis.

A: Skull X-ray in a two-year-old child with congenital hypothyroidism shows wide anterior fontanelle, mild brachycephaly, underdeveloped skull base, increased bone density, underdeveloped paranasal sinuses, slightly hypoplastic facial bones, enlarged sella turcica, wormian bones, narrowed diploic space of parietal bones, and overcrowded teeth.

B: AP view of knee demonstrates epiphyseal dysgenesis of lower femoral and upper tibial epiphyses and delayed appearance of the upper fibular epiphysis.

C, D: Plain X-rays of the pelvis and both hips in a two-year-old child and five-year-old demonstrate epiphyseal dysgenesis of the upper femoral epiphyses, shallow acetabular roofs, mild coxa vara deformity, and small iliac bones.

E, F: Plain X-rays of the dorsolumbar region show flattening of vertebral bodies with relative osteoporosis, "picture framing" of vertebral bodies, wide disc spaces, bullet-shaped vertebral bodies, and smooth gibbus deformity due to anterior subluxation of DV12 over LV1.

question_text: For segmental anatomy of liver, which of the following is not used as a landmark?
explanation:
• The Couinaud classification of liver anatomy divides the liver into eight functionally independent segments.
  • Each segment has its own vascular inflow, outflow and biliary drainage.

The liver is divided in three vertical planes:

  • The plane of the right hepatic vein divides the right lobe into anterior and posterior segments.
  • The plane of the middle hepatic vein divides the liver into right and left lobes or right and left hemiliver. This plane runs from the inferior vena cava to the gallbladder fossa.
  • The umbilic plane runs from the falciform ligament to the inferior vena cava and divides the left lobe into a medial part, which is segment IV and a lateral part formed by segment II and III.
  • The portal vein divides the liver into upper and lower segments
  • Hepatic artery is not used in couinaud classification of the liver segmental anatomy.

Reference: AIIMS-MAMC-PGI's Comprehensive textbook of diagnostic radiology page number 1948

question_text: What diagnostic procedure is being illustrated in the image provided?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a barium swallow study, a specialised imaging procedure that uses barium sulfate contrast to visualise the oesophagus, pharynx, and upper gastrointestinal tract under fluoroscopic guidance. This investigation is commonly employed to assess:

  • Oesophagal narrowing or strictures
  • Achalasia (seen as a classic "bird-beak" tapering)
  • Esophageal cancer
  • Hiatal hernia
  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

Explanation for other options:

Fluoroscopy (Option A): Fluoroscopy is the imaging technique used during a barium swallow, but the test itself is not called fluoroscopy; rather, it's termed based on the anatomical focus-here, a barium swallow.

X-ray for alkali ingestion (Option C): Though alkali ingestion leads to deep tissue damage, plain X-rays are usually not diagnostic unless complications like perforation or pneumomediastinum occur. A barium study is used later to detect post-injury strictures.

X-ray for acid ingestion (Option D): Acid ingestion often damages the stomach due to coagulative necrosis. Plain abdominal X-rays are rarely helpful for early diagnosis. Follow-up contrast studies, like a barium swallow, are more useful in detecting long-term complications.

References:

  • Barium swallow | Radiology Reference Article | Radiopaedia.org
  • Normal indentations on the oesophagus in barium swallow
  • Definition of barium-meal photofluorography - NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms
  • Barium Tests (Barium Meal, Swallow, Follow Through)
  • Double contrast barium enema technique | Radiology Reference Article

question_text: Which radioisotope is commonly used in PET-CT scans?
explanation:
Explanation:

18F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose) is the most commonly used radiotracer in PET-CT imaging. It is a glucose analogue labelled with Fluorine-18 and accumulates in tissues with high glucose metabolism, such as cancer cells, inflammation, or infection. This allows PET-CT to detect, stage, and monitor cancers, as well as assess treatment response.

Mechanism:

  • Cancer cells rely on glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen (Warburg Effect).
  • 18F-FDG enters cells via GLUT-1 transportersand is phosphorylated, trapping it inside the cell.
  • Tumour heterogeneity, size, and microvasculature can affect uptake.

Applications:

Diagnosis and staging of cancers (e.g., lung, oesophageal)

  • Detection of distant metastases
  • Monitoring response to therapy (reduced FDG uptake indicates effective treatment)

Explanation for Other Options:

Iodine (Option B): Radioactive iodine (I-123, I-131) is primarily used for thyroid imaging and treatment of thyroid disorders.

Radium (Option C): Radium-223 is used therapeutically for bone metastases, particularly in prostate cancer.

Caesium-131 (Option D): Caesium-131 is employed in brachytherapy for localised radiation delivery, such as in prostate cancer.

Reference:

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0009926010001790

question_text: A patient presented with difficulty swallowing solid foods, with no problem swallowing liquids. A barium swallow examination was performed. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a thin, shelf-like filling defect projecting into the lumen of the upper (cervical) esophagus with mild dilation of the proximal segment, which is characteristic of esophageal web.

Esophageal Webs:

Esophageal webs are thin mucosal membranes that cause constriction within the esophagus, often leading to narrowing of the lumen. While many patients remain asymptomatic and may discover the condition incidentally, severe cases can result in significant symptoms such as dysphagia and regurgitation of food.

Location:

  • Cervical Esophagus: Esophageal webs are more commonly found in the cervical region, particularly near the cricopharyngeus muscle.
  • Characteristics:
    • Typically arise from the anterior wall of the esophagus.
    • They do not originate from the posterior wall but can be circumferential.

Fluoroscopy: Barium Swallow

  • Demonstration: Esophageal webs can often be visualized on high-volume barium swallow studies when the esophagus is fully distended.
  • "Jet Effect": A characteristic "jet effect" may be observed, where contrast material passes distal to the web, indicating the presence of the membrane.

Esophageal carcinoma (Option A):

  • On barium swallow, shows irregular narrowing or apple-core lesion due to wall infiltration.
  • Causes progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids.
  • Not a thin, shelf-like defect as seen in a web.

Esophageal stricture (Option B):

  • Appears as a smooth, tapered narrowing of the lumen, often in the distal esophagus.
  • May be due to reflux, corrosive injury, or post-radiation changes.
  • Dysphagia is progressive, affecting both solids and liquids, unlike the intermittent solid dysphagia of a web.

Zenker's diverticulum (Option D):

  • Seen as a posterior outpouching just above the upper esophageal sphincter on barium swallow.
  • Associated with regurgitation of undigested food and coughing after swallowing, which are not features of an esophageal web.

Key Takeaways:

  • Esophageal web: thin, anterior mucosal membrane; typically cervical esophagus.
  • Causes solid dysphagia, often intermittent.
  • Associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

question_text: What is shown in the ultrasound image given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Key Features in Liver Examination:

  • Liver Parenchyma:
    • Echo Texture: Normal liver tissue appears homogeneous and slightly more reflective compared to the adjacent renal cortex.
  • Vascular Anatomy:
    • Portal Vein:
      • Branches radiate from the hilum of the liver.
      • Increased wall reflectivity is noted.
      • Normal waveform is continuous and antegrade, with a mean peak velocity of approximately 15 to 25 cm/s.
      • Variability in flow may occur with respiration and the cardiac cycle.
    • Hepatic Veins:
      • Converge on the inferior vena cava (IVC) and right atrium.
      • Walls are typically indistinguishable from adjacent liver parenchyma.
      • Doppler examination reveals a waveform that reflects right heart pressure changes, showing transient flow reversal during the cardiac cycle.

Spleen (Option A):

  • Normal Appearance:
    • Location: Located in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen, posterior to the stomach and above the left kidney.
    • Hilum: The hilum is the area where blood vessels and lymphatic vessels enter and exit the spleen, visible on ultrasound.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Splenomegaly: An enlarged spleen can indicate various conditions, such as infections, liver disease, hematological disorders, or malignancies.
    • Trauma: Ultrasound can detect splenic lacerations or hematomas, which are critical in trauma assessments.
    • Lesions: The ultrasound can help identify cysts, abscesses, or tumors within the spleen.

Testes (Option B):

  • Testes are paired oval structures with a homogeneous, low-to-moderate echogenic pattern contained within the scrotum.
  • Clinical Significance: US is used to evaluate conditions such as testicular torsion, tumors, and hydrocele.

Pancreas (Option D):

  • Normal Anatomy: The head, body, and tail are identifiable. The duct of Wirsung may be seen as a thin echogenic line.

Key Takeaway:

Abdominal ultrasound (US) is a key diagnostic tool for evaluating liver health.

Transducer and Frequency

  • Transducer Type: Phased array transducers
  • Operating Frequency: 3 to 5 MHz
  • Doppler Capability: Includes spectral Doppler, color Doppler, and harmonic imaging.

Pseudokidney sign, crescent-in-doughnut sign.

  • Target sign on USG.
  • Bowel-within-bowel appearance on CT.

question_text: Probable diagnosis of the given IVP image is?
explanation:
Image description:

There is focal terminal dilatation of bilateral ureters are seen. Also known as a "Cobra head appearance".

  • The term ureterocele means saccular dilatation of the intramural portion of ureter as it passes through the bladder wall.
  • It may be of two types-simple (orthotopic) and ectopic.
  • The ureters of a simple ureterocele drain a nonduplex kidney and insert into the bladder at their normal position at the trigone.
  • An ectopic ureterocele frequently occurs in a duplex kidney. In complete duplication, the ureter of the upper moiety generally inserts at a lower/ectopic location. This ureter is generally affected with ureterocele (the lower moiety, on the other hand is predisposed for VUR).
  • Morphologically, ureteroceles can be completely intravesical or extravesical-where the dilated portion extends outside the UB to involve the distal ureter.
  • Ureterocele typically appear on urography and cystography as smooth, rounded or ovoid filling defect in the bladder. The major concern with ureterocele is obstruction, stasis, and UTI. Hence, treatment is directed toward relieving the obstruction using cystoscopy, partial nephrectomy for the nonfunctioning upper moiety and/or ureteric reimplantation for refluxing ureter of lower moiety.

Incorrect choices explanation:

Choice B: Genitourinary TB in ureter shows Dilatation-due to atony and prolonged bacilluria

  • Long segment strictures-most commonly at distal one-third
  • Beaded/corkscrew ureter
  • "Pipe stem ureter"-rigid shortened ureter with narrow lumen
  • Ureteral calcifications (uncommon)

Choice C: VUR: diffuse dilatation of ureters seen. usually seen on MCU study, dilated ureters with associated renal pelvis dilatation of varying grades.

Choice D: Ureteric calculus seen as a filling defect on the IVP study with or without proximal dilatation of the ureter.

Key takeaway:

  • The term ureterocele means saccular dilatation of the intramural portion of ureter as it passes through the bladder wall.
  • "Cobra head appearance"

question_text: Identify the rib that is shown in the X-ray.
explanation:
Explanation:

The rib that is shown in the X-ray is the posterior part of the 3rd rib.

  • The posterior portion of the 3rd rib is identified based on its proximity to the vertebrae and its relatively horizontal orientation, which is more evident on a lateral X-ray view.
  • On imaging, this part of the rib lies closer to the spine and appears more curved and parallel to the vertebral column.
  • The highlighted structure in the image matches these features, confirming it as the posterior part of the 3rd rib.

question_text: 34-year-old male complaints of lower back pain for six months. He is previously diagnosed as a case of ulcerative disease of the colon. X-ray picture of the lumbar spine given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The given xray shows bamboo spine due to osteophyte formation which is suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic, progressive inflammatory arthritis which chiefly involves the synovial joints of the spine along with the adjacent soft tissues as well as the sacroiliac joints, although peripheral, large joints such as the hips, shoulders and knee can also be involved.

Radiological features:

SI joints: The classic sacroiliitis is bilateral and symmetrical. Changes occur in both the synovial along with ligamentous (superior and posterior) parts of the sacroiliac joints.

The earliest radiographic findings occur in the subchondral cortex which appears blurred or lost.

Later, small (rat-bite) erosions appear which are worse along the iliac aspect of the joint. These cause widening of the joint space with hazy margins. This is followed by larger erosions, subjacent sclerosis and joint space narrowing as irregular new bone bridges the joint space with eventual ankylosis and resolution of the sclerosis.

The modified New York criteria is used for grading of sacroiliitis and was established in 1994.

Spine: Spinal involvement classically starts at the dorsolumbar or lumbosacral junction.

Erosions initially occur at the vertebral margins at the site of attachment of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus (Romanus lesions) with adjacent sclerosis (shiny corner sign).

Healing of these erosions or laying down of bone beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament causes "squaring" of the vertebral bodies, best appreciated on lateral radiographs of the lumbar spine.

Exuberant new bone formation may even cause anterior convexity of the vertebral body (barrel-shaped vertebrae).

Ossifications may be seen in the interspinous ligaments and facet joints causing the dagger and tram-track signs respectively.

Facet joint ankylosis is the major factor causing loss of spinal mobility.

Dagger sign

Tram Track/Trolley sign

KEY TAKEAWAY: Radiological findings in Ankylosing Spondylitis.

Calcification of anterior longitudinal ligament.

Calcification of intervertebral disc giving rise to bamboo spine//Tram track sign/Trolley sign.

Calcification of interspinous ligament-dagger sign

On MRI-lesions seen in the anterior part of intervertebral disc [Andersson lesion].

Reference: AIIMS-MAMC-PGI's Comprehensive textbook of diagnostic radiology, page no 2184

question_text: A 65 year old lady with backache and a lateral radiograph of the spine is shown, most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Spondylolisthesis denotes the slippage of one vertebra relative to the one below.

Although it is directionless and could be applied to both anterolisthesis and retrolisthesis, in practice, spondylolisthesis is used synonymously with anterolisthesis. Often, particularly in the lower lumbar spine, it is due to spondylolysis (pars interarticularis defects).

Classification

To determine the grade of spondylolisthesis using the Meyerding classification, two vertical lines are drawn along the posterior cortex superior and inferior vertebra, and a measurement is taken between them (A). The length of the inferior vertebral body is also measured (B). A calculation of A/B determines the grade 4:

  • grade I: 0-25%
  • grade II: 26-50%
  • grade III: 51-75%
  • grade IV: 76-100%
  • grade V (spondyloptosis): >100%

The grades can be further grouped as 4:

  • "low-grade": grades 1 and 2
  • "high-grade": grades 3, 4 and 5

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Osteoporosis: Generalized decrease in the bone density of all bones mainly due to old age.

Choice B: Spondylolysis, commonly known as pars interarticularis defect or pars defect, is a defect in the pars interarticularis, the portion of the vertebral arch that connects the superior and inferior articular facets. It usually occurs in the lumbar spine.

Choice D: Discitis: inflammation of IV disc.

Key takeaway:

Difference between spondylolisthesis (Slippage of one vertebral body over other) and spondylolysis (pars interarticularis defects)

Reference:

Gaillard F, Walizai T, Knipe H, et al. Spondylolisthesis. Reference article, Radiopaedia.org

question_text: A middle aged women presented with postmenopausal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. She was advised to undergo a USG examination. On doing an USG, the following image was obtained. It showed an enlarged uterus with thickening endometrium. What is the next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Ultrasound shows a thickened, heterogeneously echogenic endometrial stripe, exceeding the normal postmenopausal limit (generally >4-5 mm in women not on HRT).
  • The uterus may appear mildly enlarged, but no definite focal mass or myometrial lesion (like fibroid) is seen
  • These sonographic findings are suggestive of endometrial pathology - which may include hyperplasia, polyp, or carcinoma.

Ultrasound Assessment

Timing of Imaging; Performing ultrasoundon days 5-10 of the menstrual cycleminimizes variability in endometrial thickness and provides more consistent measurements.

Premenopausal Considerations

  • Normal Endometrial Thickness:
    • Varies with the menstrual cycle stage, but generally:
      • Secretory Phase:A thickness of up to 15 mm is considered the upper limit of normal.
    • Exclusion of Hyperplasia:
      • Endometrial hyperplasia can be reliably excluded when the endometrium measures less than 8 mm.

Postmenopausal Considerations

  • Abnormal Thickness:
    • An endometrial thicknessgreater than 5 mm isconsidered abnormal and may warrant further evaluation.

Explanation of Incorrect options:

Follow up (Option A): In postmenopausal women, any bleeding with a thickened endometrium is considered abnormal and requires immediate evaluation - not observation.

Hysterectomy (Option B): Definitive surgical management (like hysterectomy) is not the first step. Diagnosis must first be confirmed histologically via biopsy or curettage.

Fibroid (Option D): Fibroids are myometrial lesions (not endometrial) and appear as well-defined, hypoechoic masses within the uterine wall - not diffuse endometrial thickening.

KEY TAKE AWAY:

  • Endometrial thickness measuring more than 15 mm in premenopausal women and more than 5 mm is considered endometrial hyperplasia,
  • which requires further investigations and should undergo endometrial biopsy to rule out malignancy.
  • Venetian blind appearance seen in adenomyosis (striate effect)

question_text: The improvement in image clarity and reduction of artifacts seen with Tissue Harmonic Imaging (THI) is based on which of the following physical principles?
option_a: Processing only the echoes returning at the original transmitted frequency.
option_b: Analyzing the frequency shifts of sound waves reflecting off moving targets.
option_c: Correcting for the attenuation of sound waves at different tissue depths.
option_d: Detecting secondary frequencies generated by non-linear sound wave propagation through tissue.
explanation:
Explanation:

Tissue Harmonic Imaging (THI) is an advanced ultrasound technique that enhances image quality by processing harmonic frequencies instead of the fundamental frequency.

The underlying principle:

  1. The ultrasound probe transmits sound waves at a specific frequency (the fundamental frequency, e.g., 2 MHz).
  2. As these waves travel through tissue, they compress and rarefy it. Sound travels slightly faster in compressed tissue and slower in rarefied tissue.
  3. This difference in speed distorts the original sine wave, a phenomenon known as non-linear propagation.
  4. This distortion creates new, higher frequencies that are integer multiples of the original frequency (e.g., 4 MHz, 6 MHz). These are the harmonics.
  5. In THI mode, the system filters out the returning fundamental frequency and creates an image using only the detected second harmonic frequency (e.g., 4 MHz).

This is advantageous because harmonics are generated deep within the tissue, bypassing superficial artifacts and clutter, leading to improved contrast and lateral resolution.

Explanation of other options:

Processing only the echoes returning at the original transmitted frequency (Option A): This describes fundamental imaging, the conventional B-mode ultrasound that THI is designed to improve upon. Fundamental imaging is more susceptible to artifacts from the body wall and superficial tissues.

Analyzing the frequency shifts of sound waves reflecting off moving targets (Option B): This describes the Doppler principle, which is used to detect and measure blood flow, not to create a higher-quality grayscale structural image.

Correcting for the attenuation of sound waves at different tissue depths (Option C): This is the function of Time Gain Compensation (TGC). TGC amplifies the weaker signals returning from deeper structures to create an image with uniform brightness, but it is not the basis of harmonic imaging.

Key Takeaways:

  • Tissue Harmonic Imaging (THI) creates images from second harmonic frequencies, not the transmitted fundamental frequency.
  • These harmonics are generated by the non-linear propagation of the sound wave through tissue.
  • The main benefits of THI are reduced artifacts, improved contrast resolution, and enhanced lateral resolution.

question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis in a 20-year-old male who presents with right flank pain, fever, and chills? The patient reports pain on passive extension of the right hip. Laboratory investigations reveal leukocytosis, and CT imaging demonstrates the findings shown below.

Explanation:

A psoas abscess is a pus collection in the iliopsoas compartment, typically presenting with fever, back/flank pain, and limping. Pain on passive hip extension (positive psoas sign) occurs due to irritation of the inflamed psoas muscle.
CT imaging demonstrates an abnormal fluid collection with irregular rim enhancement, confirming the diagnosis.

Etiology: May be primary (hematogenous) or secondary to adjacent infections (spine, bowel, kidney).

Explanation of other options:

Pyelonephritis (Option A): Bacterial infection of renal parenchyma; causes flank pain and fever, but not pain on hip extension.
CT: Enlarged kidney, thickened parenchyma, and loss of corticomedullary differentiation.

Appendicitis (Option C): Inflammation of appendix; presents with right lower abdominal pain. CT: Dilated appendix with wall thickening and surrounding mesenteric fat stranding.

Torsion of right undescended testis (Option D): Presents with nonspecific abdominal pain and vomiting. CT: Well-circumscribed isodense/heterodense mass representing the undescended testis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Psoas abscess = rim-enhancing fluid collection in iliopsoas compartment.
  • Pain on hip extension (psoas sign) is diagnostic.
  • CT is investigation of choice.

question_text: A patient with chronic constipation now presents with bleeding per rectum. Per rectal examination was normal. A CT scan is shown below. What is the expected barium enema finding in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The CT image shows an enhancing mass in the descending colon, highly suggestive of colorectal carcinoma. The barium enema typically shows an "apple core" or "napkin ring" deformity. This represents a short segment of concentric luminal narrowing with shouldered edges, characteristic of annular colorectal carcinoma.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the most common cancer of the gastrointestinal tract and one of the most frequently diagnosed malignancies in adults. A variety of predisposing factors have been identified, including:

Predisposing Factors:

  • Diet: Low fiber intake and high fat and animal protein consumption.
  • Obesity: Particularly prevalent in men.
  • Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD):
    • Ulcerative Colitis
    • Crohn Disease: Especially in bypassed loops or near chronic fistulas.
  • Asbestos Exposure
  • Family History: History of benign or malignant colorectal tumors.
  • History of Other Cancers: Endometrial or breast cancer.
  • Pelvic Irradiation
  • Ureterosigmoidostomy
  • Colonic Adenoma

Clinical Presentation:

Symptoms of CRC can be insidious, including:

  • Altered bowel habits (constipation and/or diarrhea)
  • Iron-deficiency anemia due to chronic occult blood loss

Acute manifestations may include:

  • Bowel obstruction
  • Intussusception
  • Rectal bleeding

Imaging Techniques:

  • CT Imaging: Most colorectal cancers appear as soft tissue densities that narrow the bowel lumen. Ulceration may be observed in larger masses. Mucinous tumors can appear as low-density masses, with low-density lymph nodes. Psammomatous calcifications may be present in mucinous adenocarcinoma.
  • Apple core deformity seen on Barium enema in cancer.

Saw tooth appearance (Option A): The saw tooth appearance can be seen in sigmoid colon diverticulosis. On barium enema, multiple small outpouchings (diverticula) along the sigmoid colon can create an irregular, serrated contour of the lumen, giving a "saw tooth" look.

Punched out ulcer (Option B): Punched out ulcer represents a focal mucosal defect seen in Crohn's disease, ischemic colitis, or ulcerative lesions. It is not circumferential and does not cause annular narrowing, so it differs from the apple core appearance.

Rat tail appearance (Option D): The "rat tail" appearance (also called "bird beak" appearance) is a classic barium swallow finding in achalasia cardia, not in colonic disease

question_text: A biologist is studying the roles of different types of ion channels regulating cardiac excitation. He identifies a voltage-gated calcium channel in the sinoatrial node, which is also present throughout the myocardium. The channel is activated at -40 mV of the membrane potential, undergoes voltage-dependent inactivation, and is highly sensitive to nifedipine. Which of the following phases of the action potential in the sinoatrial node is primarily mediated by ion currents through the channel that the molecular biologist is studying?
explanation:
The molecular biologist is studying L-type voltage-gated calcium channels. Calcium currents through these channels (ICa, L) primarily mediate phase 0 of the action potential in the sinoatrial node.

Depolarization in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes is mainly due to Ca2+ influx and not due to Na+ influx, unlike in other excitable tissues. Action potentials in nodal tissues differ from those in non-nodal cardiac tissues in that they lack phases 1 and 2.

  • Phase 0 is the depolarization phase, which is primarily mediated by the L-type voltage-gated calcium channels. Unlike other excitable tissues, the slope of this phase is not steep in nodal tissues.
  • Phase 1 and 2 are absent in action potentials in the nodal tissues.
  • Phase 3 is the repolarization phase, which is primarily mediated by voltage-gated potassium channels (the fast delayed rectifier IKr potassium channels and slow delayed rectifier IKs potassium channels).
  • Phase 4 is the resting membrane potential, which is primarily mediated by funny channels. Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), especially T-type voltage-gated calcium channels, also play an important role during this phase. The reduced outward K+ current also helps.

Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) are mainly of two types: L-type (long-lasting) and T-type (transient). L-type channels are expressed in nodal cells as well as throughout the myocardium. They are activated at a higher potential (-40mV) when compared to T-type channels, which are activated at a lower potential (-70mV). L-type channels are highly sensitive to dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine, while T-type channels are not sensitive to dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. Both channels undergo voltage-dependent inactivation.

Options B and C: Phase 1 and 2 are absent in the action potentials of nodal cells in the heart.

Option D: Phase 3 of the action potential of nodal cells is primarily mediated by the voltage-gated potassium channels IKr and IKs.

Reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition, Page Number 128-129.

question_text: A 40-year-old male presents with chronic, progressively worsening back pain. He also reports systemic symptoms including fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. On physical examination, there is localized tenderness over the lower thoracic and lumbar spine. MRI of the spine reveals characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Symptoms and Imaging: Characterized by chronic back pain, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. MRI often shows involvement of two or more adjacent vertebral bodies, typically affecting the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine in adults. A hallmark feature is the destruction of the intervertebral disc space and adjacent vertebrae with potential abscess formation.

  • The patient's symptoms of systemic infection (fever, night sweats, weight loss) combined with localized spinal tenderness and the typical MRI findings strongly suggest Pott's spine.

Explanation of other options:

Osteoporotic Vertebral Fracture (Option B):

  • Description: Common in older adults or those with osteoporosis, presenting typically as sudden onset of back pain after minimal trauma or even no apparent cause.
  • Why Not: The patient's systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss are not typical of osteoporotic fractures.

Metastatic Spinal Tumor (Option C):

  • Description: Can cause back pain and may involve vertebral bodies, but is more likely to cause widespread or multifocal pain and neurological deficits.
  • Why Not: Lacks specific systemic symptoms such as fever and night sweats that are associated with an infection like tuberculosis.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option D):

  • Description: A chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, leading to pain and progressive spinal stiffness.
  • Why Not: Typically lacks systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss unless there is a concurrent secondary inflammation or infection.

Skeletal Tubercular Involvement:

  • Epidemiology: Spinal TB accounts for about 40% of skeletal TB cases.
  • Pathogenesis: Typically results from hematogenous spread or contiguous spread from paravertebral lymph nodes.
  • Clinical Presentation: Symptoms include back pain, systemic signs of infection, and potential neurological complications from abscesses or spinal compression.
  • Diagnosis: MRI is crucial for visualization of the affected vertebrae. Confirmation is through aspiration of abscess or bone biopsy.
  • Treatment: Primarily involves antituberculous chemotherapy; severe cases may require surgical intervention.

Key Takeaways:

Pott's disease (spinal TB) should be suspected in patients with chronic back pain, systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), and MRI findings of vertebral destruction with possible abscess formation. Early diagnosis and anti-tubercular treatment are essential to prevent complications such as neurological deficits and spinal deformity.

Explanation:

A choledochal cyst refers to a congenital dilation of parts of the biliary tree, most often the common bile duct (CBD). Though commonly diagnosed in children, it may also be discovered in adulthood. The MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) image in this case likely reveals a fusiform or saccular dilation of the CBD, a hallmark feature of a choledochal cyst.

Common Clinical Manifestations:

  • Recurrent episodes of right upper abdominal pain
  • Jaundice, due to biliary stasis or obstruction
  • Occasionally, a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant
  • Increased lifetime risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma

Cholelithiasis (Option C): Involves gallstones within the gallbladder, with no associated dilation of the CBD. MRCP may show shadowing or echogenic foci in the gallbladder.

Choledocholithiasis (Option D): Refers to the presence of stones within the CBD. MRCP shows filling defects within the duct rather than generalised dilation.

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis of the case in the image given below?
explanation:
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is a non-invasive imaging technique that is highly effective for visualizing the biliary and pancreatic ducts, including the detection of choledocholithiasis, which is the presence of stones in the bile duct. MRCP has largely replaced ERCP as the diagnostic gold standard for choledocholithiasis due to its similar sensitivity (90-94%) and specificity (95-99%), without the risks associated with ionizing radiation, intravenous contrast, or the complications inherent in ERCP.

MRCP provides clear images that can help identify the number, size, and location of bile duct stones. It's particularly useful when strong or moderate signs of common bile duct stones are present.

KEY TAKEAWAY- MRCP is recommended for patients with symptoms suggestive of biliary obstruction, such as jaundice or pancreatitis, and when there is a need to evaluate the anatomy of the biliary tree preoperatively. It's also used when ultrasound and CT findings are inconclusive or when there's a high clinical suspicion of choledocholithiasis.

question_text: 35 year old man presenting with recurrent episodes of fever with chills and fatigue. An MRCP image is given. Diagnosis
explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an idiopathic, chronic, fibrosing inflammatory disorder affecting the biliary radicles leading to obstruction of bile ducts, cholestasis, progressing to biliary cirrhosis. It has a strong association with ulcerative colitis. It is thought to be an autoimmune process due to its association with other autoimmune disorders including mediastinal fibrosis, Sjögren syndrome, and retroperitoneal fibrosis.
ERCP, which has been the gold standard for diagnosis of PSC, is associated with risk of cholangitis following bile stasis and biliary injury because of presence of sacculations with increased stiffness of the biliary system. MRCP has been shown equivalent to ERCP for detecting and localizing the levels of obstruction in the biliary system, and can be helpful in establishing the diagnosis as well as help in planning for an intervention.

Diagnostic criteria include:

  • Typical cholangiographic abnormalities: Multifocal, intrahepatic strictures involving the biliary ducts alternating with normal-sized ducts producing a beaded appearance.
  • Clinical, biochemical, and liver histology findings: Patients present with progressive fatigue, pruritus, or jaundice. Elevated serum bilirubin and ALP is seen in most of the patients, with ALP rise at least three times the normal range. Liver biopsy shows inflammatory fibrosis (nonspecific) involving the portal tracts with a scarcity of bile ducts. Therefore, the histology is considered for confirmation only in case there is a suspicion of PSC.
  • Excluding the secondary causes of sclerosing cholangitis

Reference: AIIMS-MAMC-PGl's Comprehensive textbook of diagnostic radiology page 1981

question_text: Identify the abnormality found in the ultrasound image shown below.
explanation:
The Phrygian cap is the most common congenital anatomic variant of the gallbladder. In terms of anatomy, it refers to a folding of the fundus of the gallbladder back upon the body, giving it a distinctive 'cap-like appearance'.

Significance-wise, the Phrygian cap is generally considered to be a normal variant with no pathological significance. It is asymptomatic and does not require any treatment. However, it's important to recognize this variant in imaging studies because it can sometimes be mistaken for a pathological condition. For instance, it may simulate a mass in the liver during hepatobiliary imaging, but it is not associated with any disease and typically does not cause symptoms.

In clinical practice, awareness of the Phrygian cap is significant primarily to prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary surgical intervention, such as cholecystectomy, unless there are other indications for surgery like biliary colic or cholecystitis.

question_text: A patient presented with abdominal pain and heaviness after meals, particularly after fatty meals. An ultrasound showed dilated intrahepatic biliary radicles, and blood tests revealed raised direct bilirubin. What is the best investigation for diagnosing this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture of obstructive jaundice with dilated intrahepatic ducts on ultrasound strongly suggests choledocholithiasis, and the gold standard investigation for it is MRCP.

MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography):

  • Has become the gold standard for diagnosing choledocholithiasis.
  • Offers similar sensitivity (90-94%) and specificity (95-99%) without radiation or the risks associated with ERCP such as pancreatitis, bleeding and infection
  • Filling defects in the biliary tree are noted on thin cross-sectional T2-weighted images.

CT scan (Option A):

  • Contrast-enhanced CT has moderate sensitivity (65-88%).
  • Important subtle signs include:
    • Target sign: Central rounded density (stone) with surrounding lower attenuating bile or mucosa.
    • Rim sign: Stone outlined by a thin rim of high density.
    • Crescent sign: Low attenuation crescent of bile eccentrically outlining a stone.

CT Cholangiography:

  • Using biliary excreted contrast agents, this method has high sensitivity (88-96%) and specificity (88-98%) for choledocholithiasis
  • However, it is limited by complication rates of contrast agents and is best suited for patients with normal liver function tests.

Ultrasound (Option C):

  • Typically, the first-line investigation for biliary issues.
  • Key findings include:
    • Visualization of stones as echogenic rounded foci (size can range from 2 to over 20 mm).
    • Shadowing may be less pronounced than with gallbladder stones
    • Dilatation of the bile duct (>6 mm, increasing by 1 mm per decade after age 60; >10 mm post-cholecystectomy) and dilated intrahepatic biliary tree raise suspicion of stones.

ERCP (Option D):

ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) is primarily a therapeutic rather than diagnostic procedure.

Key points include:

  • Allows cannulation of the biliary tree, permitting stone extraction, sphincterotomy, stent placement, and management of strictures.
  • Although highly accurate, ERCP is no longer preferred as an initial diagnostic test because of its invasiveness and complication profile. It is now reserved for situations where therapeutic intervention is anticipated.
  • Complications: ERCP carries a significant rate of adverse events, such as:
    • Post-ERCP pancreatitis (most common)
    • Infections (e.g., cholangitis)
    • Bleeding
    • Perforation
    • Due to these risks, it is not used as a first-line diagnostic tool.
  • It is used after non-invasive imaging (e.g., MRCP or EUS) has confirmed the presence of choledocholithiasis or another treatable obstruction.

question_text: Identify the correct features of the investigation shown in the given image.

explanation:
Explanation:

Intravenous Urography (IVU), also called Intravenous Pyelography (IVP), is a non-invasive, contrast-based imaging technique of the renal parenchyma, pelvicalyceal system, ureters, and bladder.

  • Mechanism: Intravenous iodinated contrast is injected, filtered by kidneys, and sequential X-rays are taken to visualize both anatomical and functional information (excretion pattern, obstruction).
  • Uses:
    • Detect ureteropelvic junction obstruction
    • Demonstrate renal/ureteric calculi
    • Evaluate hydronephrosis, congenital anomalies
    • Evaluation of obstructive uropathy
  • Limitations: Replaced in most centres by CT urography; risk of contrast nephropathy and allergy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Invasive and therapeutic for bladder calculi (Option A): Cystoscopy with lithotripsy is therapeutic. IVU is diagnostic, not therapeutic.

Gold standard for bladder cancer (Option C): Cystoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for bladder cancer. An IVU may show a filling defect, but it is not the primary or definitive test.

Requires percutaneous access to the renal system (Option D): This statement describes a different procedure called an Percutaneous Nephrostography / Antegrade Pyelography. An IVU involves the injection of contrast into a peripheral vein

question_text: A 45-year-old man with metabolic syndrome undergoes a routine abdominal ultrasound. The image below shows a comparison between his liver and right kidney. Based on this finding, what is the most likely diagnosis?
option_d: Acute hepatitis with a hypoechoic pattern
explanation:
• The key finding in this ultrasound image is the increased echogenicity (brightness) of the liver parenchyma when compared to the cortex of the adjacent right kidney.
  • This is the sonographic hallmark of hepatic steatosis, commonly known as fatty liver. The accumulation of fat vacuoles within the hepatocytes causes increased reflection of the ultrasound waves, making the liver appear brighter.
  • Normally, the liver parenchyma should be isoechoic (of similar brightness) to or only slightly brighter than the renal cortex. The marked difference seen here is a classic sign of fatty infiltration. (Option C ruled out)

Explanation Of incorrect Options:

Cirrhosis with coarse echotexture (Option B): Cirrhosis is typically characterized by a heterogeneous or coarse echotexture, often with a nodular surface and features of portal hypertension. The liver in this image is diffusely and homogeneously hyperechoic, not coarse.

Acute hepatitis with a hypoechoic pattern (Option D): A hypoechoic pattern means the liver would appear darker than the kidney, which is the opposite of what is shown. A diffusely hypoechoic liver can sometimes be seen in acute hepatitis due to parenchymal edema.

Reference: AIIMS-MAMC-PGI's Comprehensive Textbook of Diagnostic Radiology, Page Number-1844.

Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease characterized by decreased bone mass and skeletal fragility.

The World Health Organization (WHO) operationally defines osteoporosis as a bone mineral density T-score less than -2.5 SD (more than 2.5 standard deviations under the young-adult mean), which is measured by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA), in postmenopausal women and men at least 50 years old.

Vertebral osteoporosis manifests as

  • Penciling of vertebrae
  • Loss of cortical bone and trabecular bone (ghost vertebra)
  • Compression fractures and vertebra plana (Genant classification of vertebral fractures)
  • Prominent vertical (primary) trabeculae with thinning of horizontal/secondary trabeculae in vertebral bodies
